content:
1. Rules
Rule: Massachusetts charitable-pledge enforceability
- Source: King v. Trustees of Boston University, Massachusetts
Supreme Judicial Court holding
- Document: CB pp 224-243
- Statement: In Massachusetts, a charitable subscription or
charitable pledge is enforceable when the claimant establishes
both a promise to give property to a charitable institution and
consideration or reliance supporting that promise
- Legal Question: When may a charitable pledge be enforced even
though it is not an ordinary contract?
- Requirements:
    1. A promise to give property to a charitable institution or
    for a charitable purpose
    2. Consideration or reliance supporting the promise
- Application: The court examines the donor’s language to
determine whether it constitutes a promise rather than merely an
expression of future intent, and then examines whether the
charity gave consideration or acted in reliance
- Exceptions: Massachusetts rejects the approach that would make
every charitable subscription binding without proof of
consideration or reliance under Restatement (Second) § 90(2)

Rule: Definition of a charitable subscription

 ----------------------------------------------------------------
                           PAGE BREAK
----------------------------------------------------------------

- Source: Textbook narrative citing Charities and Charitable
Foundations § 63
- Document: CB pp 224-243
- Statement: A charitable subscription is an oral or written
promise to perform specified acts or give real or personal
property to a charity or for a charitable purpose
- Legal Question: What type of promise qualifies as a charitable
subscription?
- Requirements: The promise must concern specified acts or
property and must be directed to a charity or charitable purpose
- Application: The definition identifies the category of
promises to which charitable-pledge rules may apply
- Exceptions: Classification as a charitable subscription does
not itself establish enforceability; the applicable jurisdiction
may additionally require consideration, reliance, or another
basis for enforcement

Rule: Promise versus unenforceable statement of intent
- Source: King v. Trustees of Boston University, Massachusetts
Supreme Judicial Court holding
- Document: CB pp 224-243
- Statement: A donor’s written statement may constitute an
enforceable promise to make a charitable gift even when the
donor initially retains legal title and intends to transfer the
property in stages
- Legal Question: Whether language describing a future gift is
sufficiently promissory to support an enforceable charitable
pledge
- Requirements:
    1. The language must reasonably communicate a commitment to
    transfer the property
    2. The surrounding document and circumstances must support
    an inference that the donor intended to bind himself rather
    than merely describe an optional future gift
- Application: The court considers the entire writing, including
language identifying the charity as repository, directing
delivery of materials, describing future transfers, and
providing for transfer at death
- Exceptions: Language that merely expresses a hope, desire, or
revocable intention may fail to establish a promise

Rule: King letter as a charitable pledge

 ----------------------------------------------------------------
                           PAGE BREAK
----------------------------------------------------------------

- Source: King v. Trustees of Boston University, Massachusetts
Supreme Judicial Court holding
- Document: CB pp 224-243
- Statement: Dr. King’s July 16, 1964 letter was sufficient to
create a jury question whether he promised to transfer absolute
ownership of his papers to Boston University
- Legal Question: Whether the letter’s language was sufficient
to submit the existence of a charitable promise to the jury
- Requirements:
    1. The letter named Boston University as repository of the
    papers
    2. It directed that papers be transferred to Boston
    University
    3. It stated Dr. King’s intention that portions of the
    deposited materials become Boston University’s absolute
    property as outright gifts
    4. It provided that all deposited materials would become
    Boston University’s property at Dr. King’s death
- Application: The jury could interpret the letter as a
commitment to transfer ownership, not merely as a mechanism
allowing Dr. King to make gifts if he later chose to do so
- Exceptions: The letter also stated that the materials
initially remained Dr. King’s legal property, so the jury had to
determine how that language interacted with the later gift
provisions

Rule: Charitable pledges and Restatement (Second) § 90(2)
- Source: Restatement (Second) § 90(2), as described in the
textbook narrative
- Document: CB pp 224-243
- Statement: Under Restatement (Second) § 90(2), a charitable
subscription or marriage settlement is binding under § 90(1)
without proof that the promise induced action or forbearance
- Legal Question: Must a charity prove consideration or reliance
to enforce a charitable subscription?
- Requirements: The promise must qualify as a charitable
subscription or marriage settlement and must otherwise fall
within the framework of § 90(1)
- Application: The provision eliminates the need to prove that
the charitable promise induced reliance or other action,
although the reading describes courts as disagreeing about
adoption of the rule
- Exceptions: Massachusetts rejected this approach in King and
continued to require consideration or reliance; even
jurisdictions adopting the approach may still require avoidance
of injustice

 ----------------------------------------------------------------
                           PAGE BREAK
----------------------------------------------------------------


Rule: Traditional consideration or reliance requirement for
charitable pledges
- Source: King v. Trustees of Boston University and the textbook
discussion of Massachusetts law
- Document: CB pp 224-243
- Statement: A charitable pledge ordinarily requires either
consideration or reliance to be enforceable under traditional
contract principles
- Legal Question: What supports enforcement of a charitable
pledge that is not an ordinary bargained-for contract?
- Requirements:
    1. A promise to make a charitable gift
    2. Consideration or reliance supporting enforcement
- Application: The charity may prove that it changed position,
incurred obligations, undertook a project, or otherwise acted
because of the promise, or may show a bargained-for exchange
where the facts support one
- Exceptions: Restatement (Second) § 90(2) would dispense with
proof of induced action or forbearance, but King states that
Massachusetts does not follow that approach

Rule: Promissory estoppel under Restatement (Second) § 90(1)

 ----------------------------------------------------------------
                           PAGE BREAK
----------------------------------------------------------------

- Source: Katz v. Danny Dare, Inc., Missouri Court of Appeals,
and the reading’s discussion of § 90
- Document: CB pp 224-243
- Statement: A promise may be enforced when the promisor should
reasonably expect it to induce action or forbearance, it does
induce such action or forbearance, and enforcement is necessary
to avoid injustice
- Legal Question: When may a promise be enforced despite the
absence of consideration?
- Requirements:
    1. A promise
    2. Action or forbearance induced by the promise
    3. Injustice that can be avoided only by enforcement of the
    promise
- Application: The court evaluates the promise, the promisor’s
expectation that it would induce reliance, the promisee’s actual
change of position, the detriment suffered, and whether
nonenforcement would produce injustice
- Exceptions: Reliance must be induced by the promise; a prior
decision or action that preceded the promise does not ordinarily
satisfy the reliance requirement

Rule: Detrimental reliance does not require an expenditure of
money
- Source: Katz v. Danny Dare, Inc. and the textbook discussion
of detrimental reliance
- Document: CB pp 224-243
- Statement: A change of position may constitute detrimental
reliance even when the promisee does not spend money or
surrender a legally enforceable right
- Legal Question: What qualifies as detrimental reliance for
promissory estoppel?
- Requirements:
    1. The promisee changes position because of the promise
    2. The change places the promisee in a materially worse
    position or creates a significant burden
    3. Enforcement is necessary to avoid injustice
- Application: Retirement, surrender of employment income,
increased work responsibilities, emotional burdens, or other
nonfinancial changes may qualify
- Exceptions: A merely beneficial or inconsequential response to
a promise may not establish detrimental reliance


 ----------------------------------------------------------------
                           PAGE BREAK
----------------------------------------------------------------

Rule: Katz’s retirement reliance
- Source: Katz v. Danny Dare, Inc., Missouri Court of Appeals
holding
- Document: CB pp 224-243
- Statement: An employee’s voluntary retirement may constitute
detrimental reliance when the employee retires in response to a
promise of a lifetime pension and gives up substantially greater
employment earnings
- Legal Question: Whether Katz’s retirement and loss of
employment income constituted detrimental reliance even though
he could have been fired
- Requirements:
    1. The employer promised a pension
    2. The employer intended Katz to rely on the promise
    3. Katz retired because of the promise
    4. Katz surrendered approximately $23,000 per year in
    earnings for a $13,000 annual pension
    5. Enforcement was necessary to avoid injustice because Katz
    could not return to full-time work
- Application: The court compared Katz’s actual choice—retiring
under the pension promise—with the position he occupied before
retirement, rather than asking whether he had a legal right to
continued employment
- Exceptions: The fact that Katz might otherwise have been fired
did not eliminate reliance because Dare negotiated with him,
made the pension promise, and induced voluntary retirement

Rule: Promissory estoppel does not require surrender of a legal
entitlement
- Source: Katz v. Danny Dare, Inc., Missouri Court of Appeals
holding
- Document: CB pp 224-243
- Statement: A promisee need not give up something to which the
promisee was legally entitled in order to establish promissory
estoppel
- Legal Question: Whether reliance is legally sufficient only
when the promisee surrenders an enforceable legal right
- Application: The relevant inquiry is whether the promisor made
a promise on which the promisee acted to the promisee’s
detriment, not whether the promisee relinquished an independent
legal entitlement

 ----------------------------------------------------------------
                           PAGE BREAK
----------------------------------------------------------------

- Exceptions: If the promisor was already legally obligated to
provide the promised benefit, promissory estoppel would
generally be unnecessary because another basis for enforcement
would exist

Rule: Reliance must follow the promise
- Source: Hayes v. Plantations Steel Co., as discussed in the
textbook narrative
- Document: CB pp 224-243
- Statement: A decision made before the promise cannot
ordinarily constitute action or forbearance induced by that
promise
- Legal Question: Whether a promise induced a change of position
when the promisee had already decided to act
- Application: The court compares the timing of the promise and
the alleged reliance; the promise must contribute to the
decision or conduct for which enforcement is sought
- Exceptions: A later promise may still be relevant if it
induces a new or additional change of position, but the reading
does not elaborate on such a situation

Rule: Injustice is an independent promissory-estoppel
requirement
- Source: Katz v. Danny Dare, Inc. and the reading’s discussion
of Restatement § 90
- Document: CB pp 224-243
- Statement: Even when a promise induces reliance, enforcement
is appropriate only when necessary to prevent injustice
- Legal Question: Whether nonenforcement would produce an
injustice that only enforcement can prevent
- Application: Relevant circumstances include the severity of
the reliance, the promisee’s ability to return to the prior
position, the promisor’s conduct, the parties’ relative power,
and whether the promisee faces a lasting loss
- Exceptions: In Bashas’, the charity completed its project
without the promised donations, incurred no binding reliance
liabilities, and did not show that enforcement was necessary to
avoid injustice


 ----------------------------------------------------------------
                           PAGE BREAK
----------------------------------------------------------------

Rule: Bashas’ charitable pledge limitation
- Source: In re Bashas’ Inc., as quoted in the textbook
narrative
- Document: CB pp 224-243
- Statement: Even if a jurisdiction adopted Restatement (Second)
§ 90(2), a charitable promise might remain unenforceable where
the claimant cannot establish injustice requiring enforcement
- Legal Question: Does eliminating proof of reliance eliminate
the need to establish injustice?
- Requirements: The claimant must still show that enforcement is
necessary to prevent injustice
- Application: The Bashas’ court considered whether
construction, donor commitments, liabilities, or the charity’s
existence depended on the pledge
- Exceptions: Completion of the project without the pledge,
absence of binding obligations, and absence of evidence that
other donors relied on the pledge weighed against enforcement

Rule: Commercial promises may be enforced through promissory
estoppel
- Source: Textbook narrative introducing promises in a
commercial context and Katz
- Document: CB pp 224-243
- Statement: Promissory estoppel is not confined to charitable
or otherwise noncommercial settings and may enforce commercial
promises when its elements are satisfied
- Legal Question: Whether promissory estoppel may apply to an
employment or pension promise lacking consideration
- Application: The doctrine may apply when an employer makes a
promise intended to induce retirement or another
employment-related change and the employee relies detrimentally
- Exceptions: The promise must still satisfy the requirements of
promise, induced reliance, and avoidance of injustice

Rule: ALI nonprofit-organization proposal § 490
- Source: American Law Institute, Principles of the Law of
Nonprofit Organizations § 490, 2009 tentative draft
- Document: CB pp 224-243

 ----------------------------------------------------------------
                           PAGE BREAK
----------------------------------------------------------------

- Statement: The proposed rule would permit a charity to recover
on a material pledge intended to be binding, subject to
fiduciary duties and fairness, and would presume that certain
oral or ambiguous pledges are binding
- Legal Question: When should a nonprofit pledge be presumed
binding despite uncertainty about consideration or reliance?
- Requirements:
    1. The pledge is material and intended to be binding
    2. Enforcement is fair under the circumstances
    3. Unless the governing board provides otherwise, the pledge
    falls within a listed circumstance
    4. The donor partially performed, served as a board member
    or officer, the charity reasonably relied to its detriment,
    or the promise induced another person to give or counted
    toward a matching gift
- Application: The proposal focuses on donor intent, partial
performance, institutional relationships, reliance, inducement
of other gifts, and fairness
- Exceptions: The charity’s decision to sue or compromise
remains subject to general fiduciary duties, and enforcement is
limited by fairness

Rule: Charitable Subscription Act proposed in Problem 3-1

 ----------------------------------------------------------------
                           PAGE BREAK
----------------------------------------------------------------

- Source: Textbook hypothetical legislation
- Document: CB pp 224-243
- Statement: The proposed Act would make certain charitable
subscriptions binding without consideration if they satisfy
specified writing and disclosure requirements
- Legal Question: What legal consequences would follow from
adopting a statutory formalization of charitable pledges?
- Requirements:
    1. A charity-supplied written form must prominently state
    “Legally Binding Pledge” in boldface type of at least
    ten-point size on the front
    2. A pledge not made on a charity-supplied form must be
    written, signed, and contain clear language showing an
    intent to make a legally binding pledge
    3. Partial payments are completed gifts and cannot be
    revoked
- Application: The Act would replace uncertainty about
consideration and reliance with objective formal requirements
and would make oral pledges conclusively nonbinding
- Exceptions: The Act directs courts to construe doubtful
pledges as nonbinding and would apply only to pledges made after
the specified effective date

Rule: Form functions in charitable pledges
- Source: Restatement (Second) § 90 Comment b, as discussed in
the textbook
- Document: CB pp 224-243
- Statement: Enforceability may depend partly on whether the
form of the promise performs evidentiary, cautionary, deterrent,
and channeling functions
- Legal Question: Why might formalities matter when deciding
whether to enforce a charitable promise?
- Application: Writing, signatures, clear language, and
prominent disclosures can demonstrate donor intent, caution
donors, discourage opportunistic enforcement, and channel
parties toward reliable forms
- Exceptions: The reading describes differing approaches and
does not establish one universally controlling form requirement

2. Case Narrative

 ----------------------------------------------------------------
                           PAGE BREAK
----------------------------------------------------------------

King v. Trustees of Boston University
Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr., an alumnus of Boston University’s
graduate program, owned correspondence, manuscripts, papers,
awards, and other materials of historical interest. In 1963,
Boston University began planning to expand its library’s special
collections, and Howard Gotlieb, the newly appointed director of
special collections, sought to obtain Dr. King’s papers. Other
universities, including Morehouse College, Dr. King’s
undergraduate alma mater, also approached him about the papers.
Dr. King believed Boston seemed to be the safest and best
location for the papers, but he was concerned that placing them
at Boston University might draw criticism because the papers
would be taken away from a historically Black institution in the
South. The volatile conditions in the South during the 1960s
influenced his decision. On July 16, 1964, from Atlanta,
Georgia, Dr. King sent Boston University a signed letter naming
the university’s library as the repository of his
correspondence, manuscripts, papers, awards, and other
materials. He authorized the immediate removal of most of the
materials to Boston University and stated that additional files
should be sent after each calendar year.
The letter stated that the materials would initially remain Dr.
King’s legal property, but it also stated that he intended each
year to identify materials that would become Boston University’s
absolute property as outright gifts until all had been given to
the university. It further stated that all materials deposited
with Boston University would become the university’s absolute
property upon Dr. King’s death. The papers were delivered to
Boston University in July 1964 and remained in its library’s
special collection.
After Dr. King’s death, Coretta Scott King, both individually
and as administratrix of his estate, claimed that the estate—not
Boston University—owned the papers. She sued Boston University
for conversion, alleging that the university wrongfully retained
property belonging to the estate

Katz v. Danny Dare, Inc.
I. G. Katz worked for Danny Dare, Inc. and its predecessor
companies beginning in 1950. He held several positions,
including executive vice president and sales manager, and served
on the company’s board of directors, although he was no longer a
director when he retired. Danny Dare’s president, Harry
Shopmaker, was Katz’s brother-in-law.

 ----------------------------------------------------------------
                           PAGE BREAK
----------------------------------------------------------------

In February 1973, while Katz was opening a Dare-operated store,
he placed a bag of company money near the cash register. A man
entered, took the money, and left. Katz pursued him and was
struck in the head while attempting to recover the money. Katz
was hospitalized. Although he returned to work, he had an
impaired walk, memory loss, and difficulty functioning at his
prior level. Shopmaker and others observed mistakes that caused
Dare considerable expense.
Shopmaker concluded that Katz could no longer be retained as an
effective employee and decided to negotiate a pension that would
induce him to retire. Katz was sixty-five when injured and did
not want to retire because he believed he could continue
performing useful work. His earnings were approximately $23,000
per year. Over approximately thirteen months, Shopmaker
negotiated with Katz about retirement. Shopmaker first offered
$10,500 annually, which Katz rejected. While Katz was on
vacation, Shopmaker sent a letter proposing a $13,000 annual
pension and adding Katz’s anticipated Social Security benefits
and possible part-time earnings to show that retirement could
produce approximately $1,000 more annual income than continued
employment.
Katz accepted the pension proposal. On May 22, 1975, Dare’s
board of directors unanimously adopted a resolution promising to
pay Katz $500 every two weeks, or $13,000 per year, for as long
as he lived. The resolution described Katz as a loyal employee
of more than twenty-five years and stated that he had requested
retirement because of failing health. Katz retired on June 1,
1975, at age sixty-seven, and Dare began paying the pension.
Katz later worked part-time for another company three or four
half-days per week. At Shopmaker’s request, he also worked
one-half day per week for Dare for approximately two and
one-half years. In July 1978, Dare sent Katz a check for $250
rather than $500. Katz returned the check and asserted that he
was entitled to the full payment. Dare then stopped making
payments. Shopmaker claimed that Katz’s improved health and
part-time work showed that he could work. Katz claimed that
Shopmaker demanded he work half-days five days per week or
accept a reduced pension. Katz testified that at age seventy he
could not work full-time.
Katz sought payment of the promised lifetime pension. He argued
that he had retired and surrendered substantially greater
employment income in reliance on Dare’s promise

3. Cases

 ----------------------------------------------------------------
                           PAGE BREAK
----------------------------------------------------------------

Case Name: King v. Trustees of Boston University, Supreme
Judicial Court of Massachusetts, 1995, Abrams, Justice

 ----------------------------------------------------------------
                           PAGE BREAK
----------------------------------------------------------------

- Document: CB pp 224-243
- Course: Contracts
- Facts
    - Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr. was a Boston University
    graduate-school alumnus
    - Boston University sought his papers for its expanding
    special collections library
    - Morehouse College and other universities also sought the
    papers
    - Dr. King was concerned that placing the papers at Boston
    University might be criticized as taking them away from a
    Black institution in the South
    - He nevertheless believed Boston was the safest and best
    place for the papers
    - On July 16, 1964, Dr. King signed a letter naming Boston
    University’s library as the repository of his
    correspondence, manuscripts, papers, awards, and other
    materials
    - He authorized immediate delivery of most of the materials
    and contemplated annual delivery of additional files
    - The letter stated that the materials initially remained
    his legal property
    - The letter also stated that he intended each year to make
    portions of the materials Boston University’s absolute
    property as outright gifts until all had been given
    - The letter provided that all deposited materials would
    become Boston University’s property upon his death
    - The papers were delivered to Boston University in July
    1964 and remained in its special collection
    - Coretta Scott King sued Boston University individually and
    as administratrix of Dr. King’s estate for conversion
    - She claimed that the estate, rather than Boston
    University, held title to the papers
- Procedural Posture
    - Massachusetts trial court: jury verdict found that Dr.
    King promised in the July 16, 1964 letter to transfer
    absolute title to the papers to Boston University and that
    the promise was enforceable as a charitable pledge supported
    by consideration or reliance; jury found that the letter was
    not a contract and therefore did not reach
    statute-of-limitations or laches defenses
    - Direct appeal: Plaintiff-Appellant Coretta Scott King
    sought review in the Supreme Judicial Court of Massachusetts
    on the grounds that the evidence was insufficient to
    establish an enforceable charitable pledge and that the
    trial judge should have granted judgment notwithstanding the
    verdict or a new trial
    - Supreme Judicial Court of Massachusetts:
    Plaintiff-Appellant Coretta Scott King is the appellant;
    Defendant-Appellee Trustees of Boston University are the
    appellees

 ----------------------------------------------------------------
                           PAGE BREAK
----------------------------------------------------------------

- Issue: Whether the evidence was sufficient to submit to the
jury whether Dr. King made an enforceable charitable pledge of
his papers to Boston University?
- Holding: The Supreme Judicial Court of Massachusetts held that
the evidence was sufficient to support the jury’s findings that
Dr. King promised to transfer ownership of the papers and that
the promise was supported by consideration or reliance
- Rule: Massachusetts charitable-pledge enforceability: A
charitable pledge is enforceable when there is a promise to give
property to a charitable institution supported by consideration
or reliance
- Reasoning
    - The Supreme Judicial Court treated the case as involving a
    charitable pledge because the jury found a charitable pledge
    but not a contract
    - The letter’s language could support a finding that Dr.
    King promised to transfer ownership rather than merely
    expressing an optional future intention
    - The promise to make portions of the materials Boston
    University’s absolute property as outright gifts was
    significant
    - The provision transferring all deposited materials upon
    Dr. King’s death also supported the existence of a
    commitment
    - The initial retention of legal title did not necessarily
    defeat the pledge because the letter expressly described
    later events by which ownership would pass
    - The evidence was sufficient to create a factual question
    concerning consideration or reliance by Boston University
    - The court therefore upheld submission of the
    charitable-pledge issue to the jury
- Plaintiff's/Appellee's Arguments
    - Coretta Scott King argued that the letter merely described
    an unenforceable unilateral and gratuitous method by which
    Dr. King might later give the papers
    - She argued that there was no bargained-for exchange
    binding Dr. King to the future gifts
    - She relied on the letter’s statement that the materials
    remained Dr. King’s legal property until otherwise indicated
    - She argued that Boston University could not reasonably
    rely on statements of future intent while Dr. King retained
    legal ownership
- Defendant/Appellant's Arguments
    - Boston University argued that the letter contained a
    promise to transfer ownership of the papers
    - Boston University argued that its action and reliance
    supported enforcement
    - Boston University argued that the evidence was sufficient
    for the jury to find both a promise and consideration or
    reliance
- Disposition: The Supreme Judicial Court of Massachusetts
affirmed the denial of Coretta Scott King’s motion for judgment
notwithstanding the verdict or a new trial and affirmed the
judgment for Boston University

 ----------------------------------------------------------------
                           PAGE BREAK
----------------------------------------------------------------

- Importance: King illustrates that a charitable pledge can be
enforceable even when the donor initially retains title and the
transfer is structured to occur over time. It also shows that
Massachusetts requires consideration or reliance and does not
automatically enforce every charitable subscription merely
because it is directed to a charity

Case Name: Katz v. Danny Dare, Inc., Missouri Court of Appeals,
1980, Turnage, Presiding Judge
- Document: CB pp 224-243
- Course: Contracts
- Facts
    - Katz worked for Danny Dare, Inc. and its predecessors from
    1950 until his retirement
    - He served in executive and sales positions and had been a
    member of the board of directors
    - In February 1973, Katz pursued a thief who had taken
    Dare’s money and was struck in the head
    - After hospitalization, Katz returned to work but suffered
    impaired walking, memory loss, and reduced ability to
    perform
    - Dare’s president, Harry Shopmaker, believed Katz had
    become more of a liability than an asset
    - Katz earned approximately $23,000 annually and did not
    want to retire
    - Shopmaker negotiated with Katz for approximately thirteen
    months to induce retirement
    - Shopmaker first offered $10,500 per year, which Katz
    rejected
    - Shopmaker later proposed a $13,000 annual pension and used
    Social Security and possible part-time earnings to
    demonstrate that retirement could produce slightly more
    annual income
    - Katz accepted the proposal and Dare’s board unanimously
    adopted a May 22, 1975 resolution promising $500 every two
    weeks, or $13,000 per year, for life
    - Katz retired on June 1, 1975, at age sixty-seven
    - Dare paid the pension for approximately three years
    - Katz later worked part-time for another company and
    one-half day per week for Dare
    - In July 1978, Dare sent Katz only $250 instead of $500 and
    then stopped payments after Katz rejected the reduced check
    - Dare claimed Katz’s improved health showed that he could
    work
    - Katz claimed he could not work full-time at age seventy

 ----------------------------------------------------------------
                           PAGE BREAK
----------------------------------------------------------------

- Procedural Posture
    - Associate Division of the Circuit Court: entered judgments
    for Dare in three pension-payment suits; Katz requested
    trial de novo
    - Transfer and consolidation: Katz, Plaintiff-Appellant,
    sought trial de novo in the Circuit Court, and the remaining
    case was transferred to that court; the cases were
    consolidated for a bench trial
    - Circuit Court: found that Katz did not suffer a legally
    cognizable detriment because he could have been fired and
    did not give up a legal entitlement, and entered judgment
    for Dare after the bench trial
    - Appeal of right: Plaintiff-Appellant Katz sought review in
    the Missouri Court of Appeals on the grounds that the trial
    court misapplied promissory-estoppel law and failed to
    recognize his retirement and lost earnings as detrimental
    reliance
    - Missouri Court of Appeals: Plaintiff-Appellant I. G. Katz
    is the appellant; Defendant-Appellee Danny Dare, Inc. is the
    appellee
- Issue: Whether Katz’s retirement and surrender of higher
employment earnings in reliance on Dare’s lifetime-pension
promise satisfied promissory estoppel even though Katz might
otherwise have been fired?
- Holding: The Missouri Court of Appeals held that Katz
established promissory estoppel because Dare made a pension
promise, Katz retired and gave up approximately $10,000 per year
in earnings in reliance on it, and injustice could be avoided
only by enforcing the promise
- Rule: Restatement (Second) § 90: A promise is enforceable when
it induces detrimental action or forbearance and enforcement is
necessary to avoid injustice
- Reasoning
    - The Missouri Court of Appeals identified three elements: a
    promise, detrimental reliance, and injustice avoidable only
    through enforcement
    - Dare expressly promised Katz a $13,000 annual pension for
    life
    - Dare intended Katz to rely on the promise and retire
    - Katz voluntarily retired only after the promise and gave
    up approximately $23,000 in annual employment earnings for a
    $13,000 pension
    - The fact that Katz could have been fired did not eliminate
    the significance of his actual choice to retire in response
    to the promise
    - Dare did not fire Katz but negotiated for approximately
    thirteen months and induced him to retire voluntarily
    - The trial court incorrectly focused on whether Katz
    surrendered a legal entitlement
    - Promissory estoppel protects reliance on promises that are
    not independently enforceable
    - By age seventy, Katz could not return to full-time work
    and recover the earnings he had surrendered, making
    nonenforcement unjust
    - Pitts was distinguishable because Pitts had not acted in
    reliance on a promise

 ----------------------------------------------------------------
                           PAGE BREAK
----------------------------------------------------------------

- Plaintiff's/Appellee's Arguments
    - Katz argued that Dare’s board resolution promised a
    lifetime pension
    - He argued that he would not have retired without the
    promise
    - He argued that retirement caused him to surrender
    approximately $10,000 per year compared with his prior
    earnings
    - He argued that his age and inability to work full-time
    made it impossible to return to his prior position
    - He relied on Feinberg and the Restatement’s
    promissory-estoppel doctrine
- Defendant/Appellant's Arguments
    - Dare argued that Katz faced only a choice between
    accepting the pension and being fired
    - Dare argued that Katz gave up nothing to which he was
    legally entitled
    - Dare argued that Katz had already received approximately
    $40,000 in pension payments and a paid vacation to Hawaii
    - Dare argued that Katz’s ability to work part-time
    demonstrated that continued pension payments were
    unnecessary
- Disposition: The Missouri Court of Appeals reversed the
judgments for Dare and remanded with directions to enter
judgment for Katz for the unpaid pension amounts
- Importance: Katz demonstrates that promissory estoppel can
apply in a commercial employment setting and that detrimental
reliance may consist of retirement and lost opportunities rather
than an expenditure of money. It also emphasizes that a promisee
need not surrender a legally enforceable right and that the
injustice requirement matters independently

Case Name: Hayes v. Plantations Steel Co., Supreme Court of
Rhode Island, 1982

 ----------------------------------------------------------------
                           PAGE BREAK
----------------------------------------------------------------

- Document: CB pp 224-243
- Course: Contracts
- Facts
    - Hayes had worked for the company for twenty-five years
    - He announced that he would retire in six months
    - One week before his retirement date, a company officer
    told Hayes that the company would “take care” of him
    - After Hayes retired, the company paid him a pension for
    four years
    - The company stopped payments because of financial
    conditions and a change in ownership
    - Hayes sought continued payments
- Procedural Posture
    - Trial court: ruled that the company was contractually
    bound to pay Hayes’s pension
    - Appeal of right: Defendant-Appellant Plantations Steel Co.
    sought review in the Supreme Court of Rhode Island on the
    grounds that the alleged promise lacked consideration and
    did not induce detrimental reliance
    - Supreme Court of Rhode Island: Plaintiff-Appellee Hayes is
    the appellee; Defendant-Appellant Plantations Steel Co. is
    the appellant
- Issue: Whether a promise made after Hayes had already decided
to retire induced consideration or detrimental reliance?
- Holding: The Supreme Court of Rhode Island rejected Hayes’s
contract and promissory-estoppel theories because his retirement
decision preceded the promise
- Rule: Reliance must be induced by the promise; conduct that
occurred before the promise does not ordinarily satisfy
promissory estoppel
- Reasoning: Hayes had already announced his retirement before
the company officer made the promise, so his retirement could
not have been caused by or undertaken in reliance on that
promise
- Plaintiff's/Appellee's Arguments: Hayes argued that the
company’s promise to take care of him supported continued
pension payments after his retirement
- Defendant/Appellant's Arguments: Plantations Steel argued that
Hayes had already decided to retire and therefore supplied no
consideration or reliance in response to the later promise
- Disposition: The Supreme Court of Rhode Island reversed the
trial court’s ruling for Hayes
- Importance: Hayes contrasts with Katz and highlights the
temporal requirement of promissory estoppel. Katz retired after
and because of the pension promise, while Hayes decided to
retire before receiving the company’s promise

 ----------------------------------------------------------------
                           PAGE BREAK
----------------------------------------------------------------


Case Name: In re Bashas’ Inc., United States District Court for
the District of Arizona, 2012

 ----------------------------------------------------------------
                           PAGE BREAK
----------------------------------------------------------------

- Document: CB pp 224-243
- Course: Contracts
- Facts
    - The debtors promised annual charitable contributions to a
    medical organization
    - The contributions were intended to help construct a
    medical facility called Barrow Tower
    - The charity sought payment from the debtors’ bankruptcy
    estate
    - The Barrow Tower was completed even though the debtors
    paid only a fraction of the pledged amount
    - The debtors experienced an extreme negative change in
    economic circumstances after making the pledge
    - The charity did not show that it entered binding contracts
    or incurred liabilities because of the pledge
    - The charity did not show that its existence was threatened
    by nonpayment
    - The record did not show that other donors gave because of
    the debtors’ promise
- Procedural Posture
    - Bankruptcy court: disallowed the charity’s claim after
    finding no consideration, no promissory estoppel, and no
    credible detrimental reliance
    - Appeal: Plaintiff-Appellant charitable organization sought
    review in the United States District Court for the District
    of Arizona on the grounds that the bankruptcy court should
    enforce the pledge under Restatement (Second) § 90(2)
    - United States District Court for the District of Arizona:
    Plaintiff-Appellant charitable organization is the
    appellant; Defendant-Appellee bankruptcy estate is the
    appellee
- Issue: Whether the charitable pledge was enforceable despite
the absence of consideration or substantial detrimental
reliance?
- Holding: The United States District Court for the District of
Arizona affirmed disallowance because the charity failed to
establish detrimental reliance or injustice
- Rule: Even if Restatement (Second) § 90(2) eliminates proof of
reliance for charitable subscriptions, enforcement still
requires a showing that injustice can be avoided only through
enforcement
- Reasoning: The facility was completed without the promised
donations, the charity did not incur binding obligations in
reliance, its existence was not threatened, and no other donors
were shown to have relied on the pledge

 ----------------------------------------------------------------
                           PAGE BREAK
----------------------------------------------------------------

- Plaintiff's/Appellee's Arguments: The charitable organization
argued that the promise should be binding under Restatement
(Second) § 90(2) without proof of induced action or reliance
- Defendant/Appellant's Arguments: The bankruptcy estate argued
that the pledge lacked consideration, that reliance was not
credible, and that enforcement was unnecessary to prevent
injustice
- Disposition: The United States District Court for the District
of Arizona affirmed the bankruptcy court’s disallowance of the
charitable claim
- Importance: Bashas’ shows that even a rule favorable to
charitable organizations would not make every pledge
enforceable. It preserves injustice as a limiting principle and
contrasts with King’s evidence that Boston University’s conduct
could support reliance

Case Name: Feinberg v. Pfeiffer Co., Missouri Court of Appeals,
1959
- Document: CB pp 224-243
- Course: Contracts
- Facts
    - The company’s board adopted a resolution offering Feinberg
    retirement pay of $200 per month for life
    - Feinberg retired approximately two and one-half years
    after the resolution
    - The company paid the retirement benefit for approximately
    seven years
    - The company then reduced the payment to $100 per month and
    discontinued payments after Feinberg rejected the reduction
    - Feinberg had given up employment in reliance on the
    promised pension
- Procedural Posture
    - The opinion’s full lower-court procedural history is not
    stated in the assigned reading
    - Missouri Court of Appeals: the court considered whether
    Feinberg’s reliance on the pension promise supported
    promissory estoppel
- Issue: Whether Feinberg’s retirement and surrender of
employment supported enforcement of the pension promise?
- Holding: The Missouri Court of Appeals held that reliance on
the pension promise supported enforcement
- Rule: Giving up employment in reliance on a promised pension
may constitute detrimental reliance even when the promise is not
supported by ordinary consideration

 ----------------------------------------------------------------
                           PAGE BREAK
----------------------------------------------------------------

- Reasoning: Feinberg gave up her employment because of the
promise and later became unable to obtain comparable employment;
her subsequent disability supported the conclusion that
injustice would result from nonenforcement
- Plaintiff's/Appellee's Arguments: Feinberg argued that she
retired and surrendered employment because of the promised
pension
- Defendant/Appellant's Arguments: The opposing arguments are
not stated in the assigned reading
- Disposition: The Missouri Court of Appeals enforced the
pension promise under promissory estoppel
- Importance: Feinberg supplied the principal comparison for
Katz and illustrates that retirement can be reliance even when
the employee was free to quit and the employer was free to
discharge

Case Name: Pitts v. McGraw-Edison Co., United States Court of
Appeals for the Sixth Circuit, 1964

 ----------------------------------------------------------------
                           PAGE BREAK
----------------------------------------------------------------

- Document: CB pp 224-243
- Course: Contracts
- Facts
    - Pitts was informed that the company had retired him
    - The company promised to pay him a specified percentage of
    sales thereafter
    - Pitts did not retire in response to a promise
    - He did not give up a legal entitlement or restrict his
    later activities because of the promise
- Procedural Posture
    - The opinion’s lower-court procedural history is not stated
    in the assigned reading
    - United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit:
    considered whether Pitts had acted in reliance on the
    company’s promise
- Issue: Whether Pitts took action in reliance on the company’s
promise sufficient to support promissory estoppel?
- Holding: The Sixth Circuit concluded that Pitts had not acted
in reliance on the promise
- Rule: A promise does not support promissory estoppel without
action or forbearance induced by the promise
- Reasoning: Pitts was simply informed that he had been retired
and did not change position because of a promise; the court also
applied Tennessee law, which had not adopted Restatement § 90
- Plaintiff's/Appellee's Arguments: The plaintiff’s arguments
are not stated in the assigned reading
- Defendant/Appellant's Arguments: The defendant’s arguments are
not stated in the assigned reading
- Disposition: The Sixth Circuit denied recovery under
promissory estoppel
- Importance: Pitts marks the contrast with Katz: Katz
voluntarily retired after being induced by a pension promise,
while Pitts took no action in response to the promise

4. Definitions
Charitable pledge

 ----------------------------------------------------------------
                           PAGE BREAK
----------------------------------------------------------------

- Definition: A promise to give property to a charitable
institution or for a charitable purpose
- Significance: King treats Dr. King’s letter as potentially
creating a charitable pledge rather than an ordinary contract
- Distinction: A charitable pledge may be enforceable through
reliance even when it lacks a conventional bargained-for
exchange

Charitable subscription
- Definition: An oral or written promise to perform specified
acts or give property to a charity or for a charitable purpose
- Significance: The term identifies the category of promises
addressed by Restatement (Second) § 90(2) and the casebook
discussion
- Distinction: A charitable subscription is not automatically
enforceable in Massachusetts; consideration or reliance is
ordinarily required

Consideration
- Definition: A bargained-for exchange supporting a promise
- Significance: The King jury found that the charitable pledge
was enforceable through consideration or reliance even though it
was not a contract
- Distinction: Consideration differs from reliance because
consideration is part of a bargained-for exchange, while
reliance concerns action or forbearance induced by a promise

Reliance
- Definition: Action or forbearance taken because of a promise
- Significance: Reliance supplied the possible basis for
enforcing both Dr. King’s charitable pledge and Dare’s pension
promise
- Distinction: Reliance must be caused by the promise; Hayes
demonstrates that a prior decision does not ordinarily qualify


 ----------------------------------------------------------------
                           PAGE BREAK
----------------------------------------------------------------

Detrimental reliance
- Definition: Reliance involving a change of position that
imposes a meaningful loss, burden, or disadvantage on the
promisee
- Significance: Katz’s retirement and surrender of higher
earnings constituted detrimental reliance
- Distinction: Detrimental reliance does not require an
expenditure of money or surrender of a legally enforceable right

Promissory estoppel
- Definition: A doctrine allowing enforcement of a promise when
the promise induces reliance and enforcement is necessary to
avoid injustice
- Significance: Katz applied promissory estoppel to an
employment pension promise
- Distinction: Promissory estoppel differs from contract
enforcement because it can apply without consideration

Injustice
- Definition: The unfairness that would result if a promise
inducing reliance were not enforced
- Significance: In Katz, age and inability to return to
full-time work made enforcement necessary; in Bashas’, the
absence of serious reliance made enforcement unnecessary
- Distinction: Injustice is a separate requirement from the
existence of a promise and reliance

Inter vivos gift
- Definition: A gift made during the donor’s lifetime
- Significance: The King litigation concerned whether Dr. King’s
letter created an enforceable lifetime charitable pledge
concerning materials initially delivered to Boston University
- Distinction: A completed gift differs from a promise to make a
future gift because the latter may require consideration or
reliance for enforcement


 ----------------------------------------------------------------
                           PAGE BREAK
----------------------------------------------------------------

Legal title
- Definition: Formal ownership recognized by law
- Significance: Dr. King’s letter stated that the papers
initially remained his legal property, but the Massachusetts
court held that this language did not necessarily defeat a later
promise to transfer ownership
- Distinction: Retention of legal title may coexist with a
binding promise to transfer title in the future

Completed gift
- Definition: A transfer of property that has been completed
rather than merely promised
- Significance: The proposed Charitable Subscription Act would
treat partial payments as completed gifts that could not be
revoked
- Distinction: A completed gift is different from an executory
charitable pledge that remains subject to enforceability rules

Formalities
- Definition: Required or recommended features of a promise’s
form, such as writing, signature, prominent language, or
specified type size
- Significance: The proposed Charitable Subscription Act would
use formalities to clarify donor intent and reduce litigation
- Distinction: Formalities serve evidentiary, cautionary,
deterrent, and channeling functions but do not necessarily
replace all substantive requirements unless legislation provides
that result

Commercial promissory estoppel

 ----------------------------------------------------------------
                           PAGE BREAK
----------------------------------------------------------------

- Definition: Application of promissory estoppel to promises
made in employment or other commercial settings
- Significance: Katz demonstrates that the doctrine is not
confined to charitable or noncommercial promises
- Distinction: The commercial setting does not eliminate the
requirements of induced reliance and injustice

Matching gift
- Definition: A contribution that counts toward a requirement
that another donor or funding source make a corresponding
contribution
- Significance: The ALI proposal would presume a donor intended
a pledge to be binding when the promise counted toward a
matching gift
- Distinction: A matching-gift situation may create reliance by
the charity or by other donors even if the charity has not yet
spent the pledged funds

content:
Rule: Learned Hand “Hand formula” for negligence
- Source: United States v. Carroll Towing Co., quoted in excerpt
as Judge Hand’s duty analysis using P, L, B and condition B<PL,
SOURCE: 206-277 p 208
- Document: 206-277
- Statement: Liability depends on whether the burden of adequate
precautions (B) is less than the product of the probability of
accident (P) and the gravity of resulting injury (L), stated as
B<PL
- Legal Question: When is it fair to require precautions such
that failing to take them is negligence
- Requirements:
    1. Compute whether B<PL based on three variables:
    probability of breakaway P, gravity of resulting injury L,
    and burden of adequate precautions B
- Application: Courts use this framework to decide whether a
defendant’s precautions were adequate given risk and feasibility
of prevention, such as whether a bargee should be aboard during
working daylight
- Exceptions: The opinion states there is no general rule for
all cases, and leaves open questions about custom and whether
the bargee must be aboard at night, so the Hand calculus is
applied to particular circumstances rather than mechanically
universally

Rule: Foreseeability—scope of legal responsibility depends on
foreseeability of extent vs general type
- Source: Notes section “It is generally agreed…” SOURCE:
206-277 p 206
- Document: 206-277
- Statement: A defendant is generally legally responsible for
injuries whose extent he could not reasonably have foreseen, but
it is another question whether liability attaches only if the
defendant was reasonably able to foresee the general type of
injury inflicted
- Legal Question: What degree and kind of foreseeability is
required for negligence liability to attach
- Requirements:
    1. Separate foreseeability of extent from foreseeability of
    general type
- Application: This distinction is flagged as an issue for
“scope of liability” and for assessing whether a factfinder
could find foreseeability of the relevant category of harm
- Exceptions: The notes do not resolve the rule; they identify
the open question reserved for Chapter 6

 ----------------------------------------------------------------
                           PAGE BREAK
----------------------------------------------------------------


Rule: Actor with superior skills/knowledge—circumstances taken
into account in determining reasonable care
- Source: Notes “Knowledge and Skills” quoting Restatement
(Third) § 12 with accompanying description SOURCE: 206-277 p 206
- Document: 206-277
- Statement: If an actor has skills or knowledge exceeding those
possessed by most others, those skills or knowledge are
circumstances to be taken into account in determining whether
the actor behaved as a reasonably careful person
- Legal Question: Whether and how superior knowledge/skill
affects the reasonable person standard in negligence
- Requirements:
    1. Actor has skills or knowledge exceeding those possessed
    by most others
    2. Those skills/knowledge are treated as circumstances for
    assessing reasonable care
- Application: The notes raise how the rule applies when the
expertise belongs to the plaintiff rather than the defendant,
and connect to occupation-based knowledge and skill arguments in
assessing negligence
- Exceptions: The notes clarify that special knowledge and skill
is a circumstance in negligence assessment, not a rule that
people with special skill are held to a “higher standard” in the
abstract, and emphasizes this is not automatically insurer-like

Rule: Barge owner duty during working daylight—no blanket rule
for bargee absence; liability determined by cost-benefit duty of
precautions
- Source: United States v. Carroll Towing Co., discussion of
variable-based duty and holding about requiring a bargee aboard
during working daylight SOURCE: 206-277 pp 207-208
- Document: 206-277
- Statement: There is no general rule for when bargee absence
makes a barge owner liable to other vessels if the barge breaks
away, but in cases where liability would be owed, damages are
apportioned proportionately if the injury is to the owner’s own
barge; in the circumstances at issue, it was a fair requirement
that the Conners Company have a bargee aboard during working
hours of daylight unless there was an excuse

 ----------------------------------------------------------------
                           PAGE BREAK
----------------------------------------------------------------

- Legal Question: When does bargee absence create liability to
others if barges break loose and become hazards, and how are
damages allocated
- Requirements:
    1. Assess duty as a function of: probability P of breaking
    away, gravity L of resulting injury, and burden B of
    adequate precautions
    2. Apply whether absence creates liability to others in
    context
    3. If the owner’s own barge is involved, reduce damages
    proportionately to reflect the bargee’s absence
- Application: Courts apply this as a structured approach to
duty for mooring/attendance decisions, including time-based
reasoning (daylight working hours) and contextual factors (war
activity and constant shifting in crowded harbor)
- Exceptions: The opinion leaves open whether, even in crowded
waters, a bargee must be aboard at night, and it notes the barge
must not become the bargee’s prison

Rule: Proof of custom—custom is admissible but not conclusive;
reasonable prudence standard controls
- Source: Dempsey v. Addison Crane Co., “admissible in evidence…
but it is by no means conclusive” SOURCE: 206-277 pp 259-260
- Document: 206-277
- Statement: Evidence that a practice is “prevailing” in the
industry is admissible on negligence, but neither conformity nor
nonconformity is conclusive of due care or negligence because
“strictly it is never its measure”
- Legal Question: How should evidence of industry custom be
weighed in determining negligence
- Requirements:
    1. Establish custom or prevailing practice through evidence
    and, when needed, familiarity of witnesses
    2. Still apply reasonable prudence standard rather than
    treat custom as a substitute
- Application: Parties use custom to argue what prudent people
do or what hazards are recognized, but the factfinder may still
find negligence if the custom and the “test” are not in harmony
- Exceptions: The reading notes the general rule and also
emphasizes there are rare contexts where custom may function
nearly conclusive, but the stated holding here is expressly “by
no means conclusive”

 ----------------------------------------------------------------
                           PAGE BREAK
----------------------------------------------------------------


Rule: Role split—judge decides questions of law, jury decides
questions of fact; negligence and foreseeability are mixed law
and fact typically reserved for jury
- Source: Narrative section “ESTABLISHMENT OF THE STANDARD OF
CARE: THE FUNCTION OF THE JUDGE AND THE JURY” SOURCE: 206-277 pp
218-219
- Document: 206-277
- Statement: Courts decide what legal standard applies and other
law questions, while juries decide factual observations and
evaluations; “Was a defendant negligent?” and “Was the
plaintiff’s injury reasonably foreseeable?” require applying a
legal standard to facts and normative judgment and are typically
reserved for the jury unless a policy dimension leads courts to
decide as a matter of law
- Legal Question: Who should decide negligence/foreseeability
issues, judge or jury
- Requirements:
    1. Identify whether the question is pure law, pure fact, or
    mixed law and fact
- Application: The chapter frames debates about when courts
remove mixed questions (e.g., duty) and how summary judgment or
directed verdict operates when no reasonable jury could decide
for the nonmoving party
- Exceptions: Some mixed questions are decided by the judge
(duty is described as decided by judge rather than jury), and
courts sometimes use dispositive motions as case-specific
mechanisms

Rule: When standard is clear, courts should lay it down once for
all; directed verdict appropriate in “plain” cases of conduct
outside due care
- Source: Baltimore & Ohio Railroad Co. v. Goodman, quoted
passage “But we are dealing with a standard of conduct, and when
the standard is clear it should be laid down once for all by the
Courts” SOURCE: 206-277 p 220-221
- Document: 206-277
- Statement: When the standard of conduct is clear, it should be
laid down by courts rather than left to jury in “plain” cases,
especially where nothing in the evidence relieves the actor from
responsibility
- Legal Question: Whether a negligence standard should be
decided by judge as a matter of law or left to jury as a matter
of fact in a clear situation

 ----------------------------------------------------------------
                           PAGE BREAK
----------------------------------------------------------------

- Requirements:
    1. The standard of conduct is “clear”
    2. Evidence does not suggest circumstances relieving
    responsibility
- Application: Courts may reverse and remand for judgment when a
jury verdict could not be supported under a clear standard for
due care at grade crossings
- Exceptions: The opinion recognizes that due care questions
“very generally” are for the jury but treats the case as one
governed by a clear standard

Rule: Ordinary prudent standard includes reliance on faculties
available; if vision is cut off, negligence is for jury unless
courts can say otherwise
- Source: Pokora v. Wabash Railway Co., “question… was for the
jury whether reasonable caution forbade his going forward in
reliance on the sense of hearing” and “No doubt it was his duty
to look along the track from his seat” but this does not mean
negligence as matter of law SOURCE: 206-277 pp 222-223
- Document: 206-277
- Statement: Where vision is obstructed and a traveler relies on
other faculties available, whether reasonable caution forbids
proceeding is typically for the jury; duty to look does not
automatically make going forward negligent when sight is cut
off, analogous to trusting ears at night
- Legal Question: Whether failure to look in a grade-crossing
scenario governed by obstructed view constitutes negligence as a
matter of law or presents a jury question
- Requirements:
    1. Vision is cut off by obstacles
    2. Traveler relies on other senses available
    3. Determine whether a jury could say reasonable caution
    forbade proceeding
- Application: Courts treat the “stop and look” standard as not
rigid where ordinary safeguards fail and the balance of
advantage is circumstance-dependent
- Exceptions: The opinion distinguishes Goodman facts (where
there was a clear space where train was plainly visible and
decisive failure to look), and emphasizes limiting Goodman’s
broader statement


 ----------------------------------------------------------------
                           PAGE BREAK
----------------------------------------------------------------

Rule: Negligence per se from statutory violation depends on how
the statute functions; absence of signals required by statute is
negligence in itself when unexcused
- Source: Martin v. Herzog, “It is negligence in itself” and
jurors have no dispensing power to treat statutory omission as
innocent or culpable SOURCE: 206-277 pp 228-230
- Document: 206-277
- Statement: Unexcused omission of statutory signals is more
than some evidence; it is negligence in itself because statutory
safeguards are intended for the protection of other travelers
and failing to provide them falls short of diligence required in
organized society
- Legal Question: Whether violation (or unexcused omission) of a
statute designed to protect others constitutes negligence as a
matter of law, and what jury may do with that violation
- Requirements:
    1. Existence of an admitted violation of a statute intended
    for the protection of another class
    2. Omission is unexcused (the opinion addresses unavoidable
    accident but says nomenclature question need not be resolved
    in the case)
    3. Causation remains separate: negligence is not always
    contributory negligence, and statutory violation is not
    automatically causal for all harms
- Application: Courts instruct juries that omission is
negligence and then determine causal effect, and may treat as
prima facie evidence of contributory negligence when plaintiff
violated statutory safeguard
- Exceptions: Martin distinguishes negligence from causal
connection; if illumination makes signals superfluous, offender
must prove substituted performance, otherwise causation can be
inferred prima facie; and the opinion leaves unresolved broader
questions for excused violations

Rule: Pedestrian statutory rule (keep left) is not necessarily
negligence per se when strict observance could defeat statutory
purpose under unusual conditions
- Source: Tedla v. Ellman, majority reasoning distinguishing
statutory safeguards defining additional standard vs codifying
general rule of road; statute here codifies/supplements and may
not apply inflexibly when observance would subject pedestrian to
more imminent danger SOURCE: 206-277 pp 233-237
- Document: 206-277

 ----------------------------------------------------------------
                           PAGE BREAK
----------------------------------------------------------------

- Statement: When a statute does not prescribe additional
safeguards aimed at a recognized danger but instead codifies or
supplements a common-law rule or prescribes general rule of
conduct calculated to prevent accidents, it should not be
construed as an inflexible command requiring observance even
when it would cause accidents or defeat statutory purpose;
failure without good reason remains fault, but not negligence
per se barring recovery as matter of law
- Legal Question: Whether violation of a “rule of the road”
statute by a pedestrian constitutes contributory negligence as a
matter of law
- Requirements:
    1. Characterize the statutory rule as either a direct
    safeguard against recognized dangers defining a standard, or
    as a general rule of conduct governing usual circumstances
    2. Apply limits/qualifications based on purpose and spirit
    under unusual conditions
- Application: The court evaluates whether keeping to the left
would force pedestrians into more imminent danger and whether
that would add to statutory purpose rather than serve it
- Exceptions: Pedestrian is still at fault if he fails without
good reason to observe the statutory rule; proximate cause
remains potentially for the jury where circumstances affect

Term: Negligence per se
- Definition: A doctrine where violation of a statute intended
to protect others can be treated as negligence in itself or
prima facie negligence, depending on statute type and context,
rather than requiring an independent “reasonable person”
assessment of the statutory conduct
- Significance: Central to Martin v. Herzog, Tedla v. Ellman,
Barnum v. Williams, and Perry v. S.N. as a vehicle for defining
or rejecting statutory duties and standards
- Distinction: Negligence per se is not the same as treating any
statutory violation as always dispositive; Tedla distinguishes
statutes codifying general rules from statutes prescribing
safeguards, and Perry rejects applying negligence per se when
criminal statute is not appropriate for civil duty creation

Term: “Excused violation”
- Definition: A concept in statutory negligence per se contexts
where a statutory violation may be excused so that it does not
necessarily establish negligence, based on circumstances showing
the actor behaved reasonably under the circumstances
- Significance: Appears in Barnum v. Williams instruction
dispute and interacts with emergency and reasonable conduct
discussions
- Distinction: Excused violation is not automatically limited to
“emergency” situations in Barnum, and in Tedla the statutory
rule is limited by purpose when strict observance would defeat
statutory aim

Term: Duty vs breach vs causation separation
- Definition: The reading emphasizes distinguishing negligence
characterization from proximate cause, and distinguishing
whether a statute supplies duty or merely defines breach
standards, while causation can remain contested even if
negligence is established
- Significance: Martin v. Herzog and Perry v. S.N. both stress
the significance of keeping negligence and causal connection
separate, and whether a statute is the sole source of duty
matters for negligence per se
- Distinction: Duty and breach are different from causation; a
finding of negligence does not automatically resolve whether the
statutory omission or violation actually caused the injury

Case Narrative: United States v. Carroll Towing Co. (Jan 4, 1944
sinking of barge “Anna C” off Pier 51, North River)
The United States owned the cargo of flour that was lost when
the barge “Anna C” sank off Pier 51 on the North River on
January 4, 1944. The owner of the barge was Conners Marine Co.,
Inc., and the charterer of the tug “Carroll” was Grace Line,
Inc., with the Carroll Towing Co., Inc., owning the tug. The
barge “Anna C,” along with other barges, broke loose from its
moorings while the tug “Carroll” was trying to move a nearby
barge. As a result of this breakaway, the barge eventually
collided in a way that created “collision damages” and then
sank, producing “sinking damages.”
The scenario described centers on a key human operational
factor: the bargee’s care for the barge and the consequences of
the bargee being absent. The deckhand and a harbormaster had
jointly undertaken to pass upon the “Anna C’s” fasts to the
pier, and even assuming one person’s responsibility after other
barges were added, the narrative implies the bargee was not
present to pay attention to protests or to act to inspect
injuries and call for help. The reading describes that if the
bargee had been on board, he would have gone below to examine
injury and called for help from the tug and charterer. It also
emphasizes that the tugs could have kept the barge afloat and
saved cargo until it could be beached, thus preventing sinking
damages.
In the litigation that followed, the dispute involved allocation
of damages among the parties involved in tug operations and
barge ownership, with a key question about whether a barge owner
is “slack in care” if the bargee is absent during working
daylight and what portion of damages should be assigned given
that absence contributed to the sinking damages

Case Narrative: Pitre v. Employers Liability Assurance Corp.
(Apr 29, 1967 fair baseball concession injury)

                           PAGE BREAK

A nonprofit fire department ran the annual Thibodaux Fireman’s
Fair on public school grounds in the City of Thibodaux. The fair
was designed to attract people of all ages and offered multiple
amusement attractions and foods, generating substantial net
income for the participating fire companies. One particular
concession was a baseball game at a concession stand operated as
two “alleys” under a canopy. The targets were canvas flaps or
“dolls” mounted on a rack beneath the canopy, designed to be
knocked down if struck by baseballs.
At a cost of 25 cents, participants were furnished three
baseballs from a supply kept on the counter. Participants had to
stand outside the enclosure and throw from beyond the counter;
participants were required to throw from outside the rope area
between the counter and the targets. Beneath the canopy was the
rack with flaps/dolls, and between the counter and the dolls
ropes were strung to keep spectators from walking into that
area. There were no barriers, ropes, or other devices to
restrain the thrower or isolate participants from spectators or
other patrons.
Two fire department members operated the concession from posts
inside the counter area near the restraining-side ropes and,
crucially, they did not leave to supervise patrons pitching from
the opposite side of the counter. The accident occurred around
8:00 p.m. on April 29, 1967. A fair patron, LeBouef (seventeen
years old), was winding up to pitch a baseball at the concession
when he struck the nine and one-half year old child Anthony
Pitre in the left temple region. LeBouef testified he did not
see the child prior to the accident and struck the child
inadvertently while drawing his hand behind him to pitch. The
parties disputed whether the fair operators were negligent for
failing to warn spectators and participants of dangers or for
failing to provide devices to separate and isolate participants
from others so as to prevent injury.
Following Anthony Pitre’s death, his parents (Mr. and Mrs.
Merville N. Pitre) brought suit against the insurers of the
fair, seeking damages for their son’s death by arguing the
insureds were negligent in how the baseball concession was
operated

Case Narrative: Baltimore & Ohio Railroad Co. v. Goodman (grade
crossing death of Goodman, daylight and familiarity)
A widow and administratrix of Nathan Goodman sued the railroad
after Goodman was killed by being run down at a grade crossing.
Goodman was driving an automobile truck in an easterly direction
and was killed by a train running southwesterly across the road
at a speed stated as not less than sixty miles an hour. The
collision occurred at a grade crossing and there was evidence
that the line was straight, but that Goodman’s view of beyond a
section house was limited until he was close to the crossing.
The description in the excerpt emphasizes that Goodman was
familiar with the crossing and that the accident occurred in
daylight. His speed was described as ten or twelve miles per
hour earlier and reduced to five or six miles at about forty
feet from the crossing. The respondent argued he had no
practical view beyond the section house until very close, and at
the close point the engine was still obscured. The narrative
further notes that it was thought that an emergency might have
existed and that Goodman did all he could in that emergency, as
far as the record suggests.
The legal action sought damages for death, and the railroad
defended on the ground that Goodman’s own negligence caused his
death, raising whether due care was a matter for the jury under
these grade-crossing facts or a matter of law where the standard
was clear

obstructed view killed by train, jury decides negligence)
A driver named Pokora was driving his truck west across multiple
sets of railroad tracks. At the time he approached the crossing,
the situation created obstructed sightlines: a string of boxcars
stood on the easternmost track 5–10 feet north of the crossing,
cutting off his view of the track northward. As Pokora moved
past that track, he listened for a train but heard none. The
accident occurred during daytime, but because his view was
obstructed, he could not see a train coming from the north.

When Pokora reached the primary track, he was struck by a train

between the rails of the tracks was 8 feet, but 2–3 feet were

suggests that the driver’s seat and body position left him with
a limited effective field of view northward, and that even if he
had looked from a possible alternative point (130 feet north),
the train could have been close enough at that moment that
escape would have been cut off.

listening and what he could see, and the defense insisted that
the driver should have looked and could have prevented the
accident by stopping and looking, drawing on Goodman’s
reasoning. Pokora sought relief, and the litigation raised
whether his conduct constituted negligence as a matter of law or

crash—failure to have lights)

A plaintiff and her husband were driving toward Tarrytown on the
night of August 21, 1915 in a buggy when they were struck by the
defendant’s automobile coming in the opposite direction. The
collision threw them to the ground and the husband was killed.
The collision happened at a point where the highway makes a
curve, and the defendant’s account was that the buggy emerged
from gloom. The excerpt indicates there was no evidence of
excessive speed or equipment defect and that the defendant’s
lamp beam pointed to the right as wheels turned along the curve
toward the left while the defendant peered into the shadow of
the roadway.
Negligence was charged against the defendant for not keeping to
the right of the center of the highway, based on Highway Law
provisions. Negligence was also charged against the plaintiff’s
intestate, the buggy driver, for traveling without lights under
a statute that required lights at that hour. The case was tried
to a jury, which found the defendant delinquent and the victim
blameless. The Appellate Division reversed and ordered a new
trial. The dispute then reached the U.S. system as the opinion
emphasizes correction of jury instruction regarding the legal
effect of statutory light omission.
The action sought damages for injuries resulting in death, and
the key factual and statutory dispute was whether failing to
have statutory lights was itself negligence and how the jury
should treat it given issues of causation

Case Narrative: Tedla v. Ellman (pedestrians struck by
automobile—statutory duty to walk left vs unusual danger)
Two pedestrians, Anna Tedla and her brother John Bachek, were
walking along Sunrise Highway when they were struck by a passing
automobile operated by defendant Ellman. Anna and John were
engaged in junk collection and often picked up junk at the
village incinerator. At the time of the accident, it was around
early evening on a Sunday in December when darkness had already
set in. John Bachek was deaf-mute, and he carried a lighted
lantern or at least there was testimony that he did. They were
wheeling baby carriages containing junk and wood picked up from
the incinerator.
Sunrise Highway at the location consisted of two roadways
separated by a grass plot without footpaths. There was no
footpath and the center grass plot was soft. While it is not
unlawful for a pedestrian to use the roadway under such
circumstances, pedestrians must exercise reasonable care. The
relevant Vehicle and Traffic Law required pedestrians “walking
or remaining on the paved portion, or traveled part of a
roadway” to comply with rules governing vehicles for meeting and
turning out except that pedestrians must keep to the left of the
center line and turn to their left instead of right side to
permit vehicles to pass on their right, and pedestrians were not
required to give signals as vehicles are.
The plaintiffs were proceeding in the easterly direction on the
east bound or right-hand roadway, not keeping left. Defendants
argued this statutory violation constituted contributory
negligence as a matter of law that barred recovery. Plaintiffs
offered evidence about traffic volume: few cars going east but
very heavy traffic going west, suggesting that following the
statutory left-side roadway would expose them to much more
imminent danger than proceeding on their chosen roadway. The
broader dispute was whether the statutory rule should be applied
inflexibly or whether unusual conditions can defeat negligence
per se when statutory purpose is otherwise frustrated.
The litigation sought damages for injuries and for the death of
John Bachek, and the central legal question was whether ignoring
the statutory keep-left requirement automatically bars recovery
as matter of law

    increasingly codified by the legislature due to growth in
    automobile traffic
    - It distinguished between statutes prescribing additional
    safeguards against recognized dangers (where negligence per

    general conduct rules intended for usual circumstances
    - It held courts may not give statutes effect not intended
