    - It articulated that when the statutory command is
    safety-preserving and designed for benefit of another, the
    standard of care becomes legislative fiat and omission is
    negligence as matter of law
    - But where the statute instead sets general rules of road
    that may fail under unusual conditions, negligence per se
    should not attach when strict compliance would subject the
    person to more imminent danger
    - It addressed causation: presence on the roadway where
    struck is an essential condition, but proximate cause can
    remain a question of fact for the jury given possible
    avoidance of greater risk by proceeding as plaintiffs did
    and operator’s heedlessness

violation should not constitute contributory negligence as a

- Defendant/Appellant's Arguments: Defendants argued the
plaintiffs’ failure to keep left was negligence as a matter of
law and a proximate cause of the accident
- Disposition: Court of Appeals of New York affirmed judgments
for plaintiffs
- Importance: Provides key limits on negligence per se by
distinguishing statutory safeguards from general rules of
conduct that require purpose-based exceptions

Case Narrative: Barnum v. Williams (motorcyclist collision on
rainy day—statutory negligence instruction and reasonableness)
On a rainy day, a collision occurred on Vista Avenue in Portland
between a motorcycle driven by the plaintiff (Barnum) and a car
driven by the defendant (Williams). The plaintiff was going
uphill and rounding an extremely sharp curve to his left. The
defendant was coming downhill. Vista Avenue was divided into two
lanes by a yellow line, and the line was closer to the curb on
the defendant’s side, creating a narrow lane on defendant’s
approach.
After the collision, the evidence would have supported different
interpretations of where the vehicles ended up relative to the
yellow line. The jury could have found the impact occurred on or
near the line or on the plaintiff’s side. The jury could also
have found that when the defendant observed plaintiff, plaintiff
was riding on the center line and leaning into the turn, so
defendant became apprehensive they might collide. Defendant
applied his brakes and slid into plaintiff’s lane, where
collision occurred.
The dispute on the law side focused on the trial court’s jury
instructions about “statutory negligence” and how jurors should
treat statutory violations. The instruction stated that
violation of a law is negligence in and of itself, with an
exception: if the jury found that under all attending
circumstances a statute cannot or should not be complied with by
a person exercising reasonable care for safety of himself and
others, failure to strictly observe the statute should be
excused and not deemed negligence.
The plaintiff appealed, contending the trial court gave two
erroneous instructions relating to the statutory negligence per
se doctrine and excusing instructions. The key real-world issue
was whether defendant’s statutory violation should be treated as
negligence per se or excused based on reasonable care under the
circumstances suggested by the rainy-day emergency and slipping
scenario

Two children, B.N. and K.N., attended a day care center operated
by Francis Keller and her husband Daniel Keller from March 25,
1991 to August 28, 1991. The parents of the children, S.N. and
S.N., alleged that Daniel Keller regularly abused the children
during the time they attended, both physically and sexually.
They further alleged that at least on one occasion in August
1991, when visiting the Kellers, three adults (Douglas Perry,
Janise White, and Raul Quintero) saw Daniel Keller bring a
number of children out into the adjoining home and sexually
abuse them.
The parents alleged that despite witnessing abuse, these three
individuals did not attempt to stop the abuse or report the
crimes to police or child welfare officials. They framed this as
negligence per se because Texas Family Code provisions required
any person who has cause to believe a child’s physical or mental
health or welfare has been or may be adversely affected by abuse
to report the abuse to state authorities. They also alleged
gross negligence and common-law negligence.
The legal dispute thus came from the parents’ claim that the day
care remained open and enabled ongoing abuse because Perry,
White, and Quintero knowingly failed to report suspected child
abuse as mandated by statute. The core factual controversy is
not about whether reporting was possible if they knew, but about
the statutory basis for civil duty and whether negligence per se
should be recognized based on criminal reporting provisions when
plaintiffs’ injuries occur through third-party wrongdoing

    tort exposure

    liability and laid out factors guiding the ultimate

        - whether negligence per se would impose ruinous damages

        considering broad collateral wrongdoer risk
        - whether plaintiff injury is directly or indirectly

        indirectness where injury is caused by third party’s

A male plaintiff was employed as a pile driver on a construction
project in Washington, D.C. in the excavating stage at the
corner of 12th and E Streets. The contractor rented a crane from
the defendant, a business that rented and operated cranes for
others. On March 27, 1962, the crane arrived early in the
morning and was moved onto the site excavation. The contractor’s
foreman directed the crane operator to move a welding machine
that was interfering with progress.
The crane operator and assistant proceeded to lift the welding
machine and shift it to a new location and then let it down.
Four pile drivers, including the injured plaintiff, were holding
the welding machine’s corners to prevent twisting. As the
welding machine was about to come to rest, an auxiliary jib
attached to the boom broke loose, fell, and struck two of the
pile drivers holding the corners, killing one and seriously
injuring the other who brought this lawsuit.
The legal dispute was whether the crane rental company was
negligent in two ways, including allegedly leaving the auxiliary
jib suspended when not in actual use and allegedly using unsafe
means to suspend the jib. The evidence showed the mechanism used
involved slings and open hook configurations, and there was also
alternative equipment involving shackles that would form a
closed loop attachment that was safer. The case thus centered on
whether prevailing industry practice to use the open hook slings
constituted reasonable care or whether it was unsafe given
available safer alternatives

Case Name: Dempsey v. Addison Crane Co., 247 F.Supp. 584 (D.D.C.
1965), Holtzoff, District Judge
- Document: 206-277
- Course: Torts, Week 4 — Negligence (Breach)

 ----------------------------------------------------------------
                           PAGE BREAK
----------------------------------------------------------------

- Facts
    - Male plaintiff was a pile driver employed on a
    construction project at 12th and E Streets in the Northwest
    section of Washington, D.C
    - On March 27, 1962, his employer rented a crane from
    defendant Addison Crane Co., which rented and operated
    cranes
    - Crane arrived early in the morning and was moved on site
    excavation
    - Contractor’s foreman directed crane operator to move a
    welding machine interfering with progress
    - Crane operator and assistant lifted the welding machine by
    crane, shift it, and let it down in new location
    - Four pile drivers, including plaintiff, held the machine
    corners to prevent twisting
    - As welding machine was about to come to rest, an auxiliary
    jib attached to the boom broke loose, fell, and hit two pile
    drivers
    - One pile driver was killed and the other was seriously
    injured and was the plaintiff
    - Plaintiffs claimed negligence in:
        - leaving the auxiliary jib suspended from the boom when
        not in actual use
        - unsafe means of suspending the jib
    - The boom was about 60 feet and auxiliary jib about 30 feet
    - Two slings attached jib via metal framework apertures,
    with open hooks on sling cable ends
    - One hook slipped, increasing load on lower sling, causing
    lower sling to break and jib to fall
    - Alternative safer apparatus existed using shackles forming
    closed loop instead of open hook ends
    - Evidence showed apparatus employed was prevailing in the
    industry at time, though alternative safer equipment existed
    and was used to lesser extent
    - Slings were not standard equipment and were fabricated by
    defendant in its shop
- Procedural Posture
    - U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia: Case
    tried without a jury, with the court separating liability
    from damages
    - U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia: The
    court found defendant liable on the unsafe apparatus charge
    and resumed damages trial later as described
- Issue: Whether defendant was negligent in leaving the jib
suspended and whether the attachment/suspension method for the
auxiliary jib was unsafe and caused the accident, with custom
evidence relevant to negligence
- Holding: The court found no negligence in failure to detach
and remove the jib at that moment, but found negligence in the
unsafe jib suspension apparatus because it was unsafe as of the
date of the accident and was the cause of injury

 ----------------------------------------------------------------
                           PAGE BREAK
----------------------------------------------------------------

- Rule: Dempsey v. Addison Crane Co., 247 F.Supp. 584, 260
(D.D.C. 1965), custom is admissible but not conclusive; what
ought to be done is fixed by reasonable prudence not merely by
prevailing practice
- Reasoning:
    - The court analyzed the two negligence charges separately
    - On leaving jib suspended, it concluded plaintiffs did not
    sustain by fair preponderance of evidence that failure to
    detach/removal was negligence merely because not in actual
    use at that moment
    - On unsafe apparatus charge, the court reviewed the jib
    attachment mechanism in detail
    - It addressed prevailing custom: the apparatus used was
    widely used in industry and some large concerns used it
    - It acknowledged admissibility of prevailing custom but
    stated conformity or nonconformity is not conclusive proof
    of due care
    - It cited the idea that a whole calling may lag in adoption
    of new devices, and “reasonable prudence is not common
    prudence” as strict measure
    - It concluded the means and apparatus by which jib attached
    were unsafe as of the accident date and constituted
    negligence, and that this negligence caused the injuries
- Plaintiff's/Appellee's Arguments: Defendant was negligent for
leaving jib suspended when not in use and for using unsafe
attachment means; prevailing use did not excuse unsafe design
- Defendant/Appellant's Arguments: Defendant argued it used
standard prevailing equipment practices in the crane rental
industry and thus did not breach due care
- Disposition: District court found defendant liable on unsafe
apparatus negligence and set damages to be tried later
- Importance: Provides explicit doctrinal treatment of custom
evidence, especially rejecting custom as conclusive and using
reasonable prudence rather than industry practice as measure of
negligence

-----
Case Narrative: Shilkret v. Annapolis Emergency Hospital
Association (infant brain damage, malpractice standard for
physicians and hospitals)

 ----------------------------------------------------------------
                           PAGE BREAK
----------------------------------------------------------------

An infant plaintiff, Mark Alan Shilkret, was born at Anne
Arundel General Hospital on December 22, 1968 and remained
continuously institutionalized due to brain damage allegedly
caused by intracranial bleeding at delivery. His parents sued
physicians and the hospital for negligence, alleging both
delivery and subsequent treatment failures. The case involved
multiple doctors: two obstetricians who treated the mother
during prenatal stage and delivered the infant, an
anesthesiologist at birth, and a pediatrician who allegedly
examined the infant the day after birth. The hospital was also
named.
At trial, the court ruled that the applicable medical
malpractice standard was the “strict locality” rule, requiring
plaintiffs to prove that the defendants failed to meet the
standard of care exercised by physicians in their own community
or locality. Because plaintiffs conceded they could not prove
under the strict locality rule, they requested leave to make a
proffer of expert medical testimony that could meet any other
standard and then attempted to proceed with proffered expert
testimony in support of a broader standard.
The proffered testimony described national standards: one
expert, an obstetrician-gynecologist involved with an Army
hospital and accredited-hospital affiliations, believed
accredited hospitals met national standards in caring for
obstetrical patients. Another neurosurgeon expert indicated
national standards for neurological diagnosis and treatment and
that the defendants violated national standards applicable to
child delivery, infant care, and treatment of neurological
problems. The central dispute thus became what standard of care
should govern medical malpractice in Maryland, and whether
plaintiffs could rely on national standards rather than strict
locality

Case Name: Shilkret v. Annapolis Emergency Hospital Association,
276 Md. 187 (1975), Levine, Judge
- Document: 206-277
- Course: Torts, Week 4 — Negligence (Breach)

 ----------------------------------------------------------------
                           PAGE BREAK
----------------------------------------------------------------

- Facts
    - Infant Mark Alan Shilkret born at Anne Arundel General
    Hospital on December 22, 1968
    - Infant has been continuously institutionalized since birth
    due to brain damage alleged to result from intracranial
    bleeding caused by negligence at delivery
    - Subsequent treatment by defendant physicians and hospital
    is alleged to have also contributed to the injury
    - Defendants include:
        - two obstetricians who treated mother prenatally and
        delivered infant
        - an anesthesiologist attending at birth
        - a pediatrician examining infant the day after birth
        - the hospital Anne Arundel General Hospital
    - Trial court ruled strict locality rule applies and
    directed verdict for defendants because plaintiffs could not
    meet that standard
    - Plaintiffs conceded inability to prove strict locality and
    made extensive proffers of experts to meet other standards
    - Obstetrician expert testified about American Hospital
    Association membership, Joint Commission on Accreditation
    standards, national standard compliance for accredited
    hospitals, and his role in Army hospital
    - Neurosurgeon expert testified about national standards for
    neurological diagnosis and treatment and that defendants
    violated those national standards
    - The appellate history affirmed directed verdict based on
    strict locality rule
- Procedural Posture
    - [the opinion as excerpted]: Trial court directed verdict
    for defendants under strict locality rule
    - Court of Special Appeals affirmed
    - Court of Appeals of Maryland reversed and remanded for new
    trial
- Issue: What standard of care applies in medical malpractice
cases in Maryland, including whether the strict locality rule
should govern physicians and hospitals or whether a national or
similar locality standard should apply
- Holding: Court of Appeals of Maryland rejected strict locality
and held that physicians and hospitals are held to a standard of
a reasonably competent practitioner/hospital in same class under
same or similar circumstances, taking account of advances and
availability of facilities, and held proffered evidence
sufficient to take standard-of-care issue to jury
- Rule: Shilkret v. Annapolis Emergency Hospital Association,
349 A.2d 245 (Md. 1975), duty is degree of care and skill
expected of reasonably competent practitioner in same class
under same or similar circumstances, and locality rules no
longer fit modern medicine

 ----------------------------------------------------------------
                           PAGE BREAK
----------------------------------------------------------------

- Reasoning:
    - The court explained that general negligence principles
    govern malpractice claims and plaintiffs bear burden to show
    lack of requisite skill or care
    - It emphasized specialty and specialized knowledge require
    a standard beyond the ordinary reasonably prudent lay
    person, but the standard must be fair to both patient and
    physician
    - It traced history of locality rules and criticized strict
    locality as too narrow given modern communications,
    availability of medical literature, training
    standardization, and changed medical realities
    - It discussed strict locality and similar locality rules as
    previously developed to protect rural practitioners, but
    held those rationales no longer fit
    - It explained that specialization and certification have
    established uniform requirements not governed by geography
    - It held strict locality can no longer be sustained given
    current state of medical science
    - It also addressed hospitals and found no prior distinction
    in Maryland and that accreditation and regulation impose
    statewide standards consistent with reasonable competent
    standard
    - It held that evidence of national standards for accredited
    hospitals and specialists and general practitioners was
    sufficient to send standard-of-care issue to jury as to all
    appellees
    - It limited the review to standard of care and did not
    reach whether breach and causation were proven
- Plaintiff's/Appellee's Arguments: Plaintiffs argued strict
locality rule should not apply, and proffered national standards
through expert testimony
- Defendant/Appellant's Arguments: Defendants argued strict
locality rule controls and plaintiffs failed to meet evidentiary
requirements under that rule
- Disposition: Court of Appeals of Maryland reversed directed
verdict and remanded for new trial consistent with its
standard-of-care holdings
- Importance: Updates the negligence “reasonable care” analysis
for medical malpractice by rejecting strict locality and
adopting a reasonably competent practitioner/hospital standard
incorporating national advances and facilities

Case Narrative: Helling v. Carey (glaucoma undetected in
under-40 patient—profession standard no routine pressure tests)

 ----------------------------------------------------------------
                           PAGE BREAK
----------------------------------------------------------------

Barbara Helling, the plaintiff, had primary open angle glaucoma.
Glaucoma is described as a condition where nourishing fluids do
not flow out of the eye easily, gradually raising pressure and
damaging the optic nerve fibers, with first loss usually
occurring in the periphery and often few symptoms such that it
is undetected until damage becomes extensive and irreversible
without a pressure test. The defendants were ophthalmologists
Dr. Thomas F. Carey and Dr. Robert C. Laughlin, partners
practicing ophthalmology.
Helling first consulted the defendants in 1959 for myopia and
was fitted with contact lenses. She next consulted in September
1963 concerning irritation from the contact lenses. There were
additional consultations in October 1963, February 1967,
September 1967, October 1967, May 1968, July 1968, August 1968,
September 1968, and October 1968. Until the October 1968
consultation, the defendants considered her visual problems
related solely to contact lens complications. On that October
1968 consultation, Dr. Carey tested eye pressure and field of
vision for the first time and indicated that Helling had
glaucoma.
At the time, Helling was thirty-two years old and essentially
had lost peripheral vision, with central vision reduced to
approximately 5 degrees vertical by 10 degrees horizontal.
Thereafter, in August 1969 after consulting other physicians,
she filed a complaint alleging the severe and permanent damage
resulted proximately from defendants’ negligence. Experts
testified that professional standards for ophthalmology in
similar circumstances did not require routine pressure tests for
glaucoma patients under 40, because the disease rarely occurs in
that age group. But the record also established that pressure
tests are required when complaints and symptoms reveal glaucoma
should be suspected.
The dispute became whether, despite professional standards not
requiring routine testing under-40 absent suspected signs,
reasonable prudence required earlier testing in this unique case
where a simple harmless pressure test could have detected
glaucoma and potentially avoided grave irreversible vision loss

Case Name: Helling v. Carey, 83 Wn.2d 514 (1974), Hunter,
Associate Justice
- Document: 206-277
- Course: Torts, Week 4 — Negligence (Breach)

 ----------------------------------------------------------------
                           PAGE BREAK
----------------------------------------------------------------

- Facts
    - Plaintiff Barbara Helling suffered from primary open angle
    glaucoma
    - Glaucoma causes interference with drainage of nourishing
    fluids, gradually raising eye pressure
    - Resulting pressure damages optic nerve fibers, causing
    field loss that begins peripherally
    - Disease often has few symptoms and is often undetected
    until extensive irreversible damage absent pressure test
    - Defendants were ophthalmologists Dr. Thomas F. Carey and
    Dr. Robert C. Laughlin, partners practicing ophthalmology
    - Helling first consulted defendants in 1959 for myopia;
    fitted with contact lenses
    - Consultations: September 1963 (irritation), October 1963,
    February 1967, September 1967, October 1967, May 1968, July
    1968, August 1968, September 1968, and October 1968
    - Until October 1968, defendants attributed visual problems
    solely to complications associated with contact lenses
    - October 1968: for first time Dr. Carey tested eye pressure
    and field of vision
    - Results indicated glaucoma had developed; Helling was age
    32 at diagnosis
    - By then she had essentially lost peripheral vision and
    central vision reduced to approximately 5 degrees vertical
    by 10 degrees horizontal
    - August 1969: Helling filed a complaint against the
    defendants alleging severe permanent damage proximately
    resulted from negligence
    - Experts testified standards of ophthalmology do not
    require routine pressure tests for glaucoma patients under
    40, but require tests if complaints and symptoms reveal
    glaucoma should be suspected
    - Dr. Carey testified incidence of glaucoma under 40 is less
    than 100 to one per cent (described as about one in 25,000
    or less), while over-40 incidence is 2–3 per cent
    - Testimony emphasized that a pressure test is simple,
    relatively inexpensive, has no judgment factor, results are
    definitive, and giving it is harmless if eye condition
    permits
    - The record indicated absence of evidence that the test
    could not have been timely given
- Procedural Posture
    - [the opinion as excerpted]: Trial court entered judgment
    for defendants after defense verdict
    - Court of Appeals affirmed
    - Washington Supreme Court granted review and reversed trial
    judgment and remanded for damages only
- Issue: Whether adherence to professional medical standards
that do not require routine pressure tests for under-40 patients
insulates ophthalmologists from negligence liability in the
unique factual circumstances where earlier testing could have
prevented grave irreversible harm

 ----------------------------------------------------------------
                           PAGE BREAK
----------------------------------------------------------------

- Holding: Washington Supreme Court held as a matter of law that
reasonable prudence required timely pressure testing, defendants
were negligent, and remanded for a new trial on damages only
- Rule: Helling v. Carey, 83 Wn.2d 514 (1974), where a simple,
harmless, definitive test would detect glaucoma in time to
arrest irreversible harm, reasonable prudence requires timely
testing even if the profession’s routine-standard does not
require it for under-40 patients
- Reasoning:
    - The court described the case as unique and found
    undisputed expert testimony about professional standards
    - It framed the issue as whether compliance with
    professional standard should insulate from liability where
    substantial vision was lost due to failure to give timely
    pressure test
    - It reasoned that one under-40 patient’s entitlement to the
    same protection as those over 40 requires timely detection
    for irreversible damage avoidance
    - It invoked Holmes’s and Hand’s formulation about what
    usually is done is evidence, but what ought to be done is
    fixed by reasonable prudence and courts must say what is
    required even if universal disregard by calling would not
    excuse omission for imperative precautions
    - It held reasonable prudence required timely giving of the
    simple harmless test, and finding negligence as matter of
    law was appropriate because there were no disputed facts on
    liability
    - It tied negligence to proximate result of blindness
- Plaintiff's/Appellee's Arguments: Plaintiff argued defendants
should have provided pressure testing earlier to protect her
from glaucoma damage and that expert standards as applied were
inadequate under her unique facts
- Defendant/Appellant's Arguments: Defendants argued adherence
to professional standards for under-40 should insulate liability
because routine testing is not required where incidence is low
- Disposition: Washington Supreme Court reversed trial judgment
and remanded for a new trial on damages only
- Importance: Establishes how negligence analysis can override
professional custom in a narrow, “unique case” where the
precaution is imperative and simple and the harm is severe and
irreversible

Residence is not synonymous with citizenship (Robinette v Emmons *2)
A person can reside in one state and be domiciled in another. Miss. Band of Choctaw Indians v. Holyfield, 490 U.S. 30 (1989)
Two requirements are required to acquire a new domicile, physical presence in the new state and either intention to make a home there indefinitely or the absence of an intention to make a home elsewhere. See Gilbert v. David, 235 U.S. 561, 569-70, 35 S.Ct. 164, 59 L.Ed. 360 (1915)
“A person's previous domicile is not lost until a new one is acquired”. Von Dunser v. Aronoff, 915 F.2d 1071, 1072 (6th Cir.1990)  
“Federal jurisdiction is tested according to the facts as they exist at the time an action is initiated” Television Reception Corp. v. Dunbar, 426 F.2d 174, 177 (6th Cir.1970). 
“Federal courts are courts of limited jurisdiction,” and “the burden of establishing” a jurisdictional basis “rests upon the party asserting jurisdiction.” Kokkonen v. Guardian Life Ins. Co. of Am., 114 S. Ct. 1673, 1675 (1994).

Deasy v. Louisville & Jefferson County Metropolitan Sewer District
Posture
Plaintiff sued 35 Kentucky defendants under §§ 1331 and 1332
Rule 12(b)(1) granted for lack of subject matter jurisdiction 
Sixth circuit affirmed
Jurisdiction
Deasy wanted to prove that he was a resident of Tennessee, he wanted the court to be in the Western District of Kentucky, they had 1332 jurisdiction over the sewer district claims
The defendants wanted to prove that Deasy was a Kentucky resident, meaning that he and every defendant shared a state, complete diversity would fail and the court would not have subject matter jurisdiction
Facts
Deasy claimed residence in Portland, Tennessee but listed a Louisville, Kentucky address for mail and business
His claimed Tennessee residence was half of his sister’s duplex 
He owned the home he lived in when in Kentucky
He changed his voter registration to Tennessee but never voted there and voted regularly in Kentucky before the change
He was physically present in Tennessee only on weekends 
His daughter had never attended school in Tennessee
Issue
Was Deasy a resident of Tennessee or Kentucky?
Holding
Kentucky was Deasy’s domicile, diversity jurisdiction was lacking 
Reasoning
Deasy presented no evidence inconsistent with a Kentucky domicile
A voter registration change without actual voting did not move the needle
Deasy owned a home in Kentucky while only claiming half of a duplex in Tennessee
Deasy rents his Tennessee home he inhered instead of living there
Relation to Fox Case
Deasy had Kentucky home ownership with presence in Tennessee
Deasy’s primary location was in Kentucky, Fox’s primary location was in Tennessee

Pitt Excavating, LLC v. Pitt
Posture
A Tennessee LLC sued its sole member’s ex-wife who was a Kentucky citizen for conversion and breach of fiduciary duty in the US District Court for the Middle District of Tennessee
The district court first found diversity was established
On reconsideration and an evidentiary hearing, this was dismissed for lack of jurisdictional
$22,376.42 were imposed in fees 
Facts 
Mr. Pitt lived at the Kentucky farm awarded to his ex wife in their divorce
He leased an apartment in Madison, Tennessee beginning in November 2012, held a Tennessee CDL and contractor’s license, and paid federal taxes on Tennessee earned income
His ex wife filed an eviction petition in July 2013 leading Pitt to stay exclusively at the Tennessee apartment
He never changed his voter registration from Kentucky and voted in Kentucky in 2012
In a July 2013 filing objecting to the eviction, he stated he had continued to live on the Kentucky estate since 2008
After filing his lawsuit, he signed a materialman’s lien affidavit listing the Kentucky farm as his address
He petitioned a Kentucky court to set aside the divorce decree so as to reclaim the farm
Issue
Whether Mr. Pitt had abandoned his Kentucky domicile and acquired a Tennessee domicile as of the September 10, 2013 filing date
Holding
No, Mr. Pitt remained a Kentucky citizen, diversity was absent and the case was dismissed
Reasoning
Physical presence in Tennessee was satisfied but intent as a Tennessee citizen was not
Presence that is compelled does not move domicile, “one who is in a place solely by virtue of superior force exerted by another should not be held to have abandoned his former domicile.” Stifel, 477 F.2d at 1121; see also Denlinger v. Brennan, 87 F.3d 214, 216 (7th Cir.1996)
Pitt spent two to three nights per week at the Kentucky farm which indicates that he had a continued desire to remain domiciled there
Pitt pursued actions to reclaim his old house which indicated continued attachment to Kentucky domicile
The district court found that the LLC was used to manufacture diversity
Relation to Fox Case
Fox spends one to two nights per week in Kentucky and the rest in Tennessee, under the reasoning of Pitt, the majority of nights in the old domicile is evidence of continuity
Nothing about Fox’s Kentucky presence is compelled but it is not exclusive either

Robinette v. Emmons
Posture
Defendant removed the case from state court to federal court
The court sua sponte (on its own accord) ordered a show-cause briefing to determine if the case should continue in the jurisdiction it was in
Only State Farm responded 
The court discharged the show cause order and retained the case
State Farm the defendant wanted Emmons to be a Michigan citizen 
The plaintiffs wanted Emmons to be a Kentucky defendant 
Facts
The complaint alleged that the defendant Emmons was a non-resident of Kentucky who resided in Michigan
State Farm’s notice of removal responded to the allegation with a response that Emmons was a domiciliary and citizen of Michigan 
The defendants showed the Facebook profile of Emmons saying she lived in Kentucky and is from Michigan
Proof that Emmons was not registered to vote in Kentucky and had no Kentucky driver’s license
The defendants presented an address history that showed 13 years of Michigan addresses with only 6 months of Kentucky addresses
Issue
Did the removing defendant meet the burden of establishing diversity
Holding
Yes, Emmons was a Michigan citizen, complete diversity existed and the case was retained
Reasoning
The burden is on the removing defendant 
Emmon’s long term domicile indicated she was a resident of Michigan. Courts consistently
reject such short-term, transient abnormalities as citizenship markers. See, e.g., Myrick, 764 F.3d at 664
Absence of voter registration and driver’s license indicates a desire not to acquire citizenship in Kentucky
Relation to Fox Case
Fox’s Facebook says he lives in Kentucky and he changed it when his house was finished, however the Robinette case establishes that it does not prove much because you can live on one state and intend on returning to another
In Robinette the defendant removed the case successfully and it states that the removing defendant carries the burden, meaning that in the Fox case the burden is on the tech company to prove he is not a Tennessee resident
Robinette says citizenship reflects where one plans to live in the long run, Fox told Casco he hopes to settle in Bowling Green after he marries, however that plan is contingent on something that has not happened. Also domicile is fixed as of the day that the suit was filed (July 2026) when Fox lived in Nashville, worked in Nashville ans was not engaged

Why Plaintiff sued

Housing in the state asserted against

Outcome

Pitt was a Kentucky citizen
Emmons was a Michigan citizen alone

Timeline
2019: Moves to Knoxville, TN for University
2020: Registers car in Tennessee, changes driver’s license to Tennessee
2023: Graduates, moves to Nashville, leases 118 Shelby Ave
Aug 18, 2023: Registers to vote in Davidson County
2024: Buys land near Bowling Green
August 1 2024: Votes in State Primary
November 5, 2024: Votes in General election
Feb 2026: Bowling Green house completed
March 2026: Starts electric, water, and internet to the KY House
June 5-9, 2026: Music City Pro Audio invoice, billed to Nashville address, shipped to Kentucky address
June 10, 2026: Warren County dog license issued, certified from East Nashville Veterinary clinic
June 19, 2026: Blue Anchor Room show in Nashville, Fox promoted as Kentucky’s ownership
Summer 2026: Furniture brought to house, spends 1-2 nights a week there and holidays 
July 2026: Files suit in Davidson County, defendant removes case

Discussion
A federal district court may exercise diversity jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1332(a)(1) only where the amount in controversy exceeds $75,000 and the action between citizens of different states. Diversity must be complete, meaning that no plaintiff may be a citizen of the same state as any defendant. Robinette v. Emmons, No. 7:19-CV-2-REW, 2019 WL 13212618, at *1 (E.D. Ky. Jan. 25, 2019). Because the defendant is incorporated and headquartered in Tennessee, complete diversity exists  only if Fox was a citizen of Kentucky when the suit was initiated in July 2026. A court will likely conclude that he was not. Fox established domicile in Tennessee when he purchased an apartment in Nashville that he continues to lease. He maintains an active Tennessee voter registration under which he has voted, a Tennessee driver’s license, a Tennessee vehicle registration, and a Nashville based music career. Fox dies not hold a Kentucky voter registration, driver’s license or vehicle registration. Fox has purchased a house in Bowling Green, Kentucky, however, it cannot be considered a new domicile as he only spends one to two nights per week at that residence. The motion to remand is likely to succeed.

A. The defendant bears the burden as abandoning his Tennessee domicile and acquired a new one in Kentucky

Federal courts are courts of limited jurisdiction and the burden of establishing a jurisdictional basis rests upon the party asserting jurisdiction. Robinette, 2019 WL 13212618 at *1 (citing Kokkonen v. Guardian Life Ins. Co. of Am., 114 S. Ct. 1673, 1675 (1994)). In Robinette, the court required the removing defendant to present affirmative proof of the disputed party’s citizenship in order to retain the case. This case differed from Deasy and Pitt Excavating, in which the plaintiff had invoked § 1332, thus Deasy was required to prove his domicile. Since Fox chose a Tennessee court, he does need to prove his own citizenship. 
State citizenship for diversity purposes is equated with domicile. Pitt Excavating, LLC v. Pitt, 603 F. Appx 393, 396 (6th Cir. 2015) (citing Von Dunser v. Aronoff, 915 F.2d 1071, 1072 (6th Cir. 1990)). Residence is not synonymous with citizenship. Robinette, 2019 WL 13212618, at *1 (citing Kaiser v. Loomis, 391 F.2d 1007, 1009 (6th Cir. 1968)). Meaning a person can reside in one state while being domiciled in another. To establish domicile within a particular state, a person must be physically present in the state and must have either the intention to make his home there indefinitely or the absence of intention to make his home elsewhere. Pitt Excavating,, 603 F. Appx 393 (citing Stifel v Hopkins, 477 F.2d 1116, 1120 (6th Cir. 1973)). 
Fox’s Tennessee domicile is not contestable. He moved to Tennessee in 2019 to attend the University of Tennessee, he then relocated to Nashville after graduating in 2023. He leased an apartment in Nashville, obtained a Tennessee driver’s license, registered his vehicle in Tennessee, and registered to vote in Davidson county. Under Von Dunser, Fox’s Tennessee domicile continues unless the defendant proves a Kentucky domicile replaced it. 

B. Fox’s physical presence remains predominantly in Tennessee and the Sixth Circuit hastreated presence at the original domicile as evidence of a party’s continued domicile there

Pitt Excavating presents a case where Mr. Pitt sought to prove he was domiciled in Tennessee. Mr. Pitt began to stay at an apartment in Madison, Tennessee in November 2012 but did not begin to stay there exclusively until after eviction proceedings began in July 2013. However the court found Pitt’s behavior was “highly probative of a continuing desire to remain domiciled at the Kentucky farm” because he would still spend two to three nights per week at the farm up until September 2013. The court concluded that spending four to five nights per week in Tennessee in the weeks leading up to the case not sufficient to demonstrate that he abandoned his Kentucky domicile. 
Fox’s claim is stronger than Mr. Pitt, he spends only one to two nights a week in Bowling Green and the remaining five or six days in Nashville. If residing two to three nights per week in the original domicile in the Pitt case was evidence of a continued domicile in Kentucky then Fox spending most nights in Tennessee would be strong evidence of Tennessee domicile. 
Deasy reinforces this point because the plaintiff claimed Tennessee domicile but he was physically present in Tennessee only on weekends while the home he owned was in Kentucky, 47 F. Appx 728. Ultimately the court determined that Deasy was a Kentucky domiciliary. The pattern of living for Fox is the opposite, he spends weekdays in Nashville and the weekends and holidays in Bowling Green. 

C. The defendant’s evidence establishes a second residence, not a change of domiciled

The defendant’s argument that Fox is a Kentucky resident relies on Fox’s ownership of his Bowling Green property, however, ownership of property is not domicile. In Deasy, the plaintiff owned a house and a duplex in Tennessee, however this fact was not sufficient to establish Tennessee domicile because he rented the house to someone else and trips to Tennessee were infrequent. 47 F. Appx 728. In Pitt Excavating, Mr. Pitt was determined to be a Kentucky resident even though he did not even own the property on which he resided. Pitt Excavating, 603 F. Appx 394-97. These cases both apply  the principle established in Stifel which is that proving citizenship requires showing domicile not just residence. Fox uses the Bowling Green residence only on the weekends and holidays, it only furnished minimally and has only been connected to utilities for a few months. This does not reflect a house that is being occupied as a primary residence.
Since Fox’s residence in Kentucky has been brief, this strengthens his argument as a Tennessee citizen. Courts “consistently reject short-term, transient abnormalities as citizenship markers.” Robinette, 2019 WL 13212618, at *2. In Robinette, the plaintiff’s six month address in Kentucky did not override a thirteen year pattern of residence in Michigan. Fox’s Kentucky house has been finished for only six months, while he has a pattern of residence in Tennessee since 2019.
Fox changed his Facebook profile to say that he lives in Kentucky when the house there was completed. This is addressed by Robinette, where the court considered a print-out of Emmon’s Facebook profile saying that she currently lives in Kentucky and is from Michigan, this however, was not strong enough evidence to indicate that Emmons was a Kentucky citizen. Thus Fox’s social media profile is not sufficient to establish him as a Kentucky resident especially when other factors such as voter registration, vehicle registration and living patterns point to his status as a Tennessee citizen. 
The promotional flyer for one of Fox’s shows is not sufficient evidence of Kentucky citizenship either. Fox holds that he did not create nor approve it the flyer which is credited to CSP Marketing. Stifel establishes that intent to domicile in a different state can be expressed through actions the party undertakes himself such as affidavits, registrations, opening bank accounts, etc. Since the flyer was created by a third party, this is weak evidence. 

D. Fox’s deisre to settle in Bowling Green after marrying is contingent on future plans which have not occurred yet and do not effect a change of domicile

The defendant’s strongest argument is that Fox hopes to settle in Bowling Green when he marries his girlfriend. Citizenship reflects a person’s long term plan for state of habitation rather than just current residence. Robinette, 2019 WL 13212618, at *2 (citing Myrick v. Wellpoint, Inc., 764 F.3d 662, 664 (7th Cir. 2014)). The defendant will argue that this is evidence that Fox intends for his long term residence to be Kentucky. 
This argument fails because domicile is fixed by the facts as they existed when the suit was initiated. Pitt Excavating, 603 F. Appx 396 (citing Dunbar, 426 F.2d 174, 177 (6th Cir. 1970)). As of July 2026, Fox had not proposed, was not engaged, and was not married. An intention to relocate to another state at an unspecified time in the future is not an intention to establish domicile nor does it indicate the absence of an intention to make a home elsewhere. 
Fox did not indicate that he intended to abandon Tennessee citizenship because he said he plans to live in Nashville for at least the next few years because Nashville is where his regular gigs are played and where his income comes from. He added that even after any potential move to Kentucky, he would still commute to Nashville for work. Because Fox expects to continue earning income in Tennessee indefinitely and states that he will continue living there for the coming years, he has not formed a present intention to make Kentucky his home indefinitely. 

E. Conclusion

The defendant cannot carry the burden of proving that Fox is a Kentucky citizen. Fox’s physical presence is predominately in Tennessee and exceeds the presence that Pitt had at his original domicile in Kentucky in Pitt Excavating. The objective signs of intent that the Sixth Circuit relied on in Deasy and Pitt Excavating point to Tennessee in Fox’s case. Deasy found insufficient evidence inconsistent with a Kentucky domicile. 47 F. Appx 728. Fox presents stronger evidence indicating evidence against a Kentucky domicile he has a Nashville lease, an active Tennessee voter registration, a Tennessee license, a Tennessee vehicle registration, and a music career based in Nashville. The defendant’s case for Fox being a Kentucky citizen rests upon his recently finished Bowling Green house, his social media profile, and a promoter’s flyer advertising his show. A court will likely find that Fox remains a citizen of Tennessee when the suit was initiated and that complete diversity is absent.

content:
Rules
Rule: Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 90(1)
- Source: Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 90(1), adopted by
the Maine Supreme Judicial Court in Harvey v. Dow
- Document: CB pp 217-225
- Statement: A promise that the promisor should reasonably
expect to induce action or forbearance, and that does induce
such action or forbearance, is binding when enforcement is
necessary to avoid injustice, even though the promise may
otherwise be unenforceable
- Legal Question: Whether a promise should be enforced despite
the absence of an otherwise enforceable contract
- Requirements:
1. The promisor makes a promise
2. The promisor should reasonably expect the promise to induce
action or forbearance by the promisee or a third person
3. The promise actually induces action or forbearance
4. Enforcement is necessary to avoid injustice
- Application: Courts invoke § 90 when a promise lacks ordinary
contractual enforceability, such as when consideration is
absent, but the promisee materially changes position in
foreseeable reliance on the promise
- Exceptions: The remedy may be limited as justice requires, and
enforcement is not automatic merely because the promisee
experienced some detriment

Rule: Promissory Estoppel Applies to Otherwise Unenforceable
Promises
- Source: Case holding and doctrinal statement in Harvey v. Dow,
quoting Daigle Commercial Group, Inc. v. St. Laurent
- Document: CB pp 217-225
- Statement: Promissory estoppel applies to promises that are
otherwise unenforceable and is invoked to enforce those promises
when necessary to avoid injustice
- Legal Question: Whether the absence of ordinary contractual
enforceability prevents a court from enforcing a promise

 ----------------------------------------------------------------
                           PAGE BREAK
----------------------------------------------------------------

- Requirements: The promise must satisfy the elements of
Restatement (Second) § 90
- Application: The doctrine is particularly relevant where a
promise lacks consideration or otherwise fails ordinary contract
principles but induced substantial reliance
- Exceptions: A general statement of future intent, without a
promise that reasonably induces action, is insufficient

Rule: A Promise May Be Implied From Conduct
- Source: Harvey v. Dow, relying on June Roberts Agency, Inc. v.
Venture Properties, Inc. and Nappi v. Nappi Distributors
- Document: CB pp 217-225
- Statement: A promise for purposes of promissory estoppel need
not be express and may be implied from a party’s conduct
- Legal Question: Whether conduct, without an explicit verbal
commitment, can constitute a promise
- Requirements:
1. The promisor’s conduct must manifest an intention to act or
refrain from acting in a specified way
2. The conduct must be such that the promisee is justified in
understanding that a commitment has been made
- Application: The court examines the promisor’s actions in
context, including whether the promisor approved, encouraged,
facilitated, or substantially participated in the promisee’s
reliance
- Exceptions: General statements alone may be too indefinite,
but accompanying affirmative conduct may supply the missing
specificity

Rule: Definition of Promise Under Restatement (Second) § 2(1)
- Source: Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 2(1), applied in
Harvey v. Dow
- Document: CB pp 217-225
- Statement: A promise is a manifestation of intention to act or
refrain from acting in a specified way, made so as to justify
the promisee in understanding that a commitment has been made
- Legal Question: Whether a promisor’s words or conduct
communicated a sufficiently definite commitment
- Requirements:

 ----------------------------------------------------------------
                           PAGE BREAK
----------------------------------------------------------------

1. A manifestation of intention to act or refrain from acting
2. A specified manner of action or inaction
3. Circumstances justifying the promisee’s understanding that a
commitment was made
- Application: The court assesses the objective significance of
the promisor’s words and conduct rather than relying solely on
the promisor’s later characterization of the interaction
- Exceptions: A generalized intention to give property sometime
in the future may not itself identify a sufficiently definite
commitment

Rule: General Promise Plus Conduct May Identify a Specific
Parcel
- Source: Application of Restatement (Second) § 90 in Harvey v.
Dow
- Document: CB pp 217-225
- Statement: A general promise to give land at some future time
may become an enforceable promise to convey a particular parcel
when the promisor’s affirmative conduct approves and facilitates
the promisee’s substantial improvement of a specific site
- Legal Question: Whether an indefinite general promise can
become sufficiently specific through the promisor’s conduct
- Requirements:
1. A general understanding or promise that land will be given
2. The promisee selects or occupies a particular site
3. The promisor approves or supports construction or improvement
on that site
4. The promisee makes a definite and substantial change of
position
5. Enforcement is necessary to avoid injustice
- Application: The court considers the general promise together
with actions such as approving the site, obtaining a building
permit, and helping construct the improvement
- Exceptions: If the evidence consists only of generalized
statements with no conduct connecting the promise to a
particular parcel, promissory estoppel may fail because the
promise is too indefinite

Rule: Substantial Improvements to Land May Support Enforcement
of a Promise to Convey
- Source: Harvey v. Dow, relying on Tozier v. Tozier and Nappi
v. Nappi Distributors
- Document: CB pp 217-225

 ----------------------------------------------------------------
                           PAGE BREAK
----------------------------------------------------------------

- Statement: When a donee makes substantial improvements to land
in reliance on a promise to convey the land, courts may enforce
the promise because refusing enforcement may be fraudulent,
unjust, and inequitable
- Legal Question: Whether the promisee’s improvements are
sufficiently substantial and reliance-based to justify
enforcement of a land gift
- Requirements:
1. A promise to convey land
2. Reliance on that promise
3. Substantial improvements to the land
4. Injustice or inequity if the promise is not enforced
- Application: Building a house is treated as a valuable and
permanent improvement that may establish the required reliance
- Exceptions: A mere showing that the donee incurred some
detriment at the donor’s request is insufficient without
substantial improvements made in reliance on the promise

Rule: Lack of Consideration Does Not Bar Promissory-Estoppel
Enforcement
- Source: Harvey v. Dow, quoting Nappi v. Nappi Distributors
- Document: CB pp 217-225
- Statement: A promise may be enforceable under promissory
estoppel notwithstanding the absence of consideration
- Legal Question: Whether a promise lacking consideration can
nevertheless be enforced
- Requirements: The promise and reliance must satisfy
Restatement (Second) § 90
- Application: The doctrine addresses promises that resemble
gifts but induce substantial, foreseeable, and detrimental
reliance
- Exceptions: Lack of consideration does not itself establish
promissory estoppel because substantial reliance and avoidance
of injustice are still required

Rule: Reliance on a Promise to Make a Gift Must Be Foreseeable,
Reasonable, Definite, and Substantial
- Source: Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 90 comment f,
discussed in Harvey v. Dow

 ----------------------------------------------------------------
                           PAGE BREAK
----------------------------------------------------------------

- Document: CB pp 217-225
- Statement: A promise to make a gift is ordinarily enforced
based on reliance only when the promisee’s conduct is
foreseeable and reasonable and involves a definite and
substantial change of position that would not have occurred
without the promise
- Legal Question: Whether reliance on a gratuitous promise is
sufficiently justified to warrant enforcement
- Requirements:
1. Foreseeable conduct
2. Reasonable reliance
3. A definite change of position
4. A substantial change of position
5. A causal connection between the promise and the change
- Application: The court asks whether the promisee’s conduct was
the kind of reliance the promisor should have anticipated and
whether it materially altered the promisee’s position
- Exceptions: Reliance that is trivial, speculative,
unreasonable, or unrelated to the promise may not justify
enforcement

Rule: Reasonableness of Reliance Is Generally a Fact Question
- Source: Textbook discussion of Bouton v. Byers
- Document: CB pp 217-225
- Statement: Whether reliance was reasonable is ordinarily a
fact question rather than an issue to be resolved categorically
as a matter of law
- Legal Question: Whether the promisee was justified in relying
on the promisor’s commitment under the circumstances
- Requirements:
1. The factfinder considers whether reliance was reasonable at
all
2. The factfinder considers whether the manner and degree of
reliance were reasonable
3. The factfinder considers the surrounding relationship and
circumstances
- Application: Familial relationships, the nature of the
promised property, the parties’ motivations, and the context of
the promise may affect reasonableness
- Exceptions: The reading does not identify a categorical rule
that legal education, professional status, or knowledge that an
oral promise may be unenforceable automatically makes reliance
unreasonable

 ----------------------------------------------------------------
                           PAGE BREAK
----------------------------------------------------------------


Rule: Family Relationship May Affect Reasonableness of Reliance
- Source: Textbook discussion of Harvey v. Dow, Greiner v.
Greiner, and Bouton v. Byers
- Document: CB pp 217-225
- Statement: In family disputes, the familial relationship may
support the promisee’s expectation that the promisor will
voluntarily perform, and the relationship is relevant to whether
reliance was reasonable
- Legal Question: Whether the family context changes the
assessment of the promisee’s reliance
- Requirements: The factfinder should consider the parties’
relationship together with the promise, the conduct, and the
nature of the reliance
- Application: A promisee may rely because of family loyalty,
devotion, or an expectation of voluntary family performance
rather than because the promisee believes a court could legally
compel performance
- Exceptions: Family status does not automatically establish an
enforceable promise or reasonable reliance

Rule: Detrimental Reliance Is Central to Promissory Estoppel
- Source: Textbook discussion of Harvey v. Dow, Greiner v.
Greiner, and Wright v. Newman
- Document: CB pp 217-225
- Statement: The degree of detrimental reliance may be the most
significant factor in deciding whether promissory estoppel
should be invoked
- Legal Question: Whether the promisee changed position
sufficiently to justify enforcement
- Requirements:
1. The promisee took action or refrained from acting
2. The action or forbearance was induced by the promise
3. The change of position was substantial enough to create
injustice if the promise is not enforced
- Application: Building a house, moving to another part of the
state, or refraining from seeking another source of support are
examples discussed in the reading
- Exceptions: When detriment is unclear or unsupported by
evidence, courts may be less willing to apply promissory
estoppel


 ----------------------------------------------------------------
                           PAGE BREAK
----------------------------------------------------------------

Rule: Promissory Estoppel and Equitable Estoppel Are Distinct
Doctrines
- Source: Textbook narrative on the evolution of promissory
estoppel
- Document: CB pp 217-225
- Statement: Promissory estoppel generally concerns promises,
while equitable estoppel traditionally concerns misstatements of
fact
- Legal Question: Whether the alleged basis for estoppel is a
promise or a factual misrepresentation
- Requirements:
1. Promissory estoppel requires a promise that induces action or
forbearance
2. Equitable estoppel traditionally involves a misstatement of
fact on which the other party relies
- Application: The doctrines help identify whether the case
involves an unfulfilled commitment or reliance on an inaccurate
factual representation
- Exceptions: The reading notes that some earlier courts used
equitable estoppel to enforce promises between family members
and that equitable estoppel is normally applied defensively

Rule: Charitable Subscriptions May Be Enforced Despite Weak
Bargain Analysis
- Source: Textbook narrative introducing charitable
subscriptions
- Document: CB pp 217-225
- Statement: Courts have often found consideration in
charitable-subscription cases, although commentators regard many
such analyses as unconvincing and view promissory estoppel as a
possible basis for enforcement
- Legal Question: Whether a promise to make a charitable
contribution should be enforced when ordinary bargain-based
consideration is absent or unclear
- Requirements: The reading does not provide a complete
charitable-subscription test
- Application: Promissory estoppel may provide courts a way to
enforce charitable promises without creating an artificial
finding that a true bargain occurred
- Exceptions: The assigned material introduces the topic but
does not provide the following case or a complete rule governing
charitable subscriptions

Case Narrative

 ----------------------------------------------------------------
                           PAGE BREAK
----------------------------------------------------------------

Teresa L. Harvey is the daughter of Jeffrey Dow Sr. and Kathryn
L. Dow, and Jeffrey B. Dow Sr. and Kathryn L. Dow are the
defendants in the dispute. Teresa’s brother, Jeffrey Dow Jr.,
also lived on the family property. The family owned 125 acres in
Corinth, Maine, divided into adjoining fifty-acre and
seventy-five-acre parcels. Teresa, her brother, and their
parents each had homes on the property
From childhood, Teresa and Jeffrey Jr. discussed the homes they
would someday build on the family homestead. Teresa wanted her
home near a spring, close to the location where she ultimately
built it. The Dows viewed the property as their children’s
heritage and expected that some or all of it would eventually be
left or given to Teresa and Jeffrey Jr. Jeffrey Sr. testified
that when the children were teenagers, he believed Kathryn had
promised them land in the future, and the subject of the
children living on the homestead was commonly discussed within
the family
In 1999, Teresa and her future husband, Jarrod Harvey, placed a
mobile home on the Dows’ land with permission. The mobile home
was located where Jeffrey Jr.’s mobile home is now located.
Teresa paid no rent and did not ask for a deed. She and Jarrod
later built a garage near the mobile home, again with the Dows’
permission
Around January 2003, Teresa and Jarrod decided to build a
permanent house on the lot where their mobile home stood. At
their request, the Dows agreed to use their home-equity line of
credit to provide initial financing. Teresa testified that
repayment was supposed to include the Dows’ conveying the
building site to her by deed once the house was completed,
although Jeffrey Sr. denied that a deed was discussed at that
time
Jarrod died in a motorcycle accident in March 2003. After his
death, Teresa decided to finance the house with life-insurance
proceeds instead of using the Dows’ home-equity line of credit.
Before construction, Teresa, Jeffrey Sr., and Teresa’s
grandfather determined that moving the house farther back on the
property would cost no more than building at the mobile-home
location. The new location was near the spring where Teresa had
always wanted to build. Jeffrey Sr. agreed that she could build
there
Teresa and Jeffrey Sr. went to the town to obtain a building
permit. The town initially denied a permit because Teresa lacked
the required road frontage, but a permit was eventually issued
to Jeffrey Sr. for him to build another house on his property.
Teresa testified that Jeffrey Sr. told her he would execute a
deed after the house was built, while Jeffrey Sr. testified that
no deed was discussed

 ----------------------------------------------------------------
                           PAGE BREAK
----------------------------------------------------------------

Construction began in summer 2003 and finished in May 2004, at a
cost to Teresa of approximately $200,000. Jeffrey Sr. performed
substantial construction himself, including much of the
foundation work and carpentry, and helped arrange underground
electrical lines. Teresa moved into the completed house
In January 2004, while the house was being built, Teresa lent
$25,000 to her brother. By spring 2004, around the time the
house was completed, the family relationship had deteriorated
over repayment of the loan and over the Dows’ dissatisfaction
with Teresa’s partner, who lived with her. Teresa eventually
sued Jeffrey Jr. for repayment, and the Dows filed a
grandparents’ rights action concerning Teresa’s children
After moving into the house, Teresa asked Jeffrey Sr. for a deed
so that she could obtain a mortgage for other projects. After
discussions, it became clear that the Dows would not execute a
deed. Teresa paid taxes on the house itself but did not pay the
property taxes on the land or any rent. Kathryn Dow and Jeffrey
Jr. testified that they did not know of any offer or agreement
by Jeffrey Sr. to deed land to Teresa
Teresa filed a complaint seeking to compel the Dows to convey
the land on which her house stood or to award damages based on
the value of the house. She also asserted claims including
breach of contract, breach of fiduciary duty, and fraud
Cases
Case Name: Harvey v. Dow, Maine Supreme Judicial Court, 962 A.2d
322 (2008), Mead, J
- Document: CB pp 217-225
- Course: Contracts
- Facts
- Teresa L. Harvey was the daughter of Jeffrey Dow Sr. and
Kathryn L. Dow
- The Dows owned 125 acres in Corinth, Maine, in adjoining
fifty-acre and seventy-five-acre parcels
- Teresa, her brother Jeffrey Jr., and their parents each had
homes on the property
- Teresa and her brother had discussed since childhood the homes
they wanted to build on the homestead
- The family generally understood that the land was the
children’s heritage and that Teresa and Jeffrey Jr. would
eventually receive some or all of it
- Teresa and Jarrod installed a mobile home on the property in
1999 with the Dows’ permission, paid no rent, and did not
request a deed
- Teresa and Jarrod later built a garage with permission
- Around January 2003, they planned to build a permanent house

 ----------------------------------------------------------------
                           PAGE BREAK
----------------------------------------------------------------

- Teresa testified that the Dows’ financing plan included a deed
conveying the building site after completion, while Jeffrey Sr.
denied discussing a deed
- Jarrod died in a motorcycle accident in March 2003
- Teresa then planned to finance construction with
life-insurance proceeds
- Teresa, Jeffrey Sr., and Teresa’s grandfather selected the
house’s eventual location farther back on the property near the
spring
- Jeffrey Sr. approved that location
- The town initially denied a permit because Teresa lacked
sufficient road frontage
- A permit was eventually issued to Jeffrey Sr. for construction
of another house on his property
- Teresa testified that Jeffrey Sr. promised to execute a deed
after construction, while Jeffrey Sr. denied that any deed was
discussed
- Construction began in summer 2003 and was completed in May
2004
- Teresa spent approximately $200,000 on the house
- Jeffrey Sr. performed substantial construction work and helped
arrange underground electrical lines
- Teresa lent $25,000 to Jeffrey Jr. in January 2004
- Family relationships deteriorated over repayment of the loan
and the Dows’ dissatisfaction with Teresa’s partner
- Teresa eventually sued Jeffrey Jr. over the loan, and the Dows
filed a grandparents’ rights action concerning Teresa’s children
- Teresa later requested a deed so she could obtain a mortgage
for other projects
- The Dows did not execute a deed
- Teresa paid taxes on the house but not the property taxes on
the land or rent
- Kathryn Dow and Jeffrey Jr. denied knowing of an agreement to
deed land to Teresa
- Procedural Posture
- Superior Court of Penobscot County: found for the Dows on
Teresa’s real-property claims and on the Dows’ request for a
declaratory judgment after a two-day bench trial
- Appeal of right: Plaintiff-Appellant Teresa Harvey sought
review in the Maine Supreme Judicial Court on the grounds that
the Superior Court failed to address or properly apply
promissory estoppel and the possible effect of the Dows’ conduct
- Maine Supreme Judicial Court: Teresa Harvey is the appellant;
Jeffrey B. Dow Sr. and Kathryn L. Dow are the appellees

 ----------------------------------------------------------------
                           PAGE BREAK
----------------------------------------------------------------

- Issue: Whether the Dows’ general statements that Teresa would
receive land, combined with their approval and assistance in
building her substantial house on a particular parcel, could
support an enforceable promise under promissory estoppel
- Holding: The Maine Supreme Judicial Court held that the
Superior Court erred by considering only the Dows’ generalized
statements and failing to consider their affirmative conduct,
because a promise to convey the specific site could be implied
from approving the location, obtaining a building permit, and
substantially helping construct the house
- Rule: Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 90(1): A promise
that the promisor should reasonably expect to induce action or
forbearance, and that does induce such action or forbearance, is
binding when enforcement is necessary to avoid injustice, and
the remedy may be limited as justice requires
- Reasoning:
- The Maine Supreme Judicial Court accepted the finding that the
Dows made general promises that Teresa would eventually receive
some land as a gift or inheritance
- A general promise alone would be too indefinite because the
parties had not specified the parcel’s size, boundaries, or time
of conveyance
- The case also involved the Dows’ acquiescence, support, and
encouragement of construction on a particular site
- Jeffrey Sr. approved the location, obtained a building permit
that facilitated construction, and performed substantial
construction work himself
- A promise may be implied from conduct when the conduct
manifests an intention to act in a specified way and justifies
the promisee in understanding that a commitment was made
- Teresa’s construction of an immobile house costing
approximately $200,000 was foreseeable and reasonable reliance
in the circumstances
- The house was a valuable and permanent improvement, making
refusal to enforce the implied promise potentially fraudulent,
unjust, and inequitable
- The absence of consideration did not prevent enforcement under
promissory estoppel
- The Superior Court therefore needed to evaluate the Dows’
conduct together with their general statements
- Plaintiff's/Appellee's Arguments: Teresa argued that the Dows’
general promises to convey land, together with their permission,
encouragement, and assistance in constructing a $200,000 house
on the property, created an enforceable promise under promissory
estoppel
- Defendant/Appellant's Arguments: The Dows argued that there
was no enforceable promise because they had not agreed on the
size, boundaries, or timing of any conveyance, and Jeffrey Sr.
denied discussing or promising a deed

 ----------------------------------------------------------------
                           PAGE BREAK
----------------------------------------------------------------

- Disposition: The Maine Supreme Judicial Court vacated the
judgment and remanded for further proceedings addressing the
Dows’ conduct, the implied promise, and the application of
Restatement (Second) § 90
- Importance: Harvey illustrates that promissory estoppel can
enforce a promise to make a gift of land even without
consideration, and that the promise may be implied from conduct
rather than stated expressly
- Importance: The case emphasizes that courts must analyze the
entire course of conduct, not merely isolated statements,
especially when the promisee makes a valuable and permanent
improvement to land
- Importance: The case also demonstrates that a general family
understanding may become sufficiently specific when the promisor
directs and assists the promisee’s reliance on a particular
parcel
- Importance: The later history reported in the reading states
that the Superior Court initially denied relief on remand
because the timing of performance was unclear, but the Maine
Supreme Judicial Court later held that the facts showed an
implicit promise of a present conveyance and directed entry of
judgment for Teresa, with the remedy to be determined under
Restatement (Second) § 90 and Comment d

Definitions
Promissory Estoppel
- Definition: A doctrine enforcing a promise when the promisor
should reasonably expect it to induce action or forbearance, it
does induce that reliance, and enforcement is necessary to avoid
injustice
- Significance: It provides a basis for enforcement even when
ordinary contract principles would not enforce the promise
- Distinction: Unlike ordinary bargain-based contract
enforcement, promissory estoppel does not require consideration

Promise
- Definition: A manifestation of intention to act or refrain
from acting in a specified way, made so as to justify the
promisee in understanding that a commitment has been made
- Significance: The promise element is central to promissory
estoppel and may be established by words or conduct

 ----------------------------------------------------------------
                           PAGE BREAK
----------------------------------------------------------------

- Distinction: A general expression of future intent may be
insufficient, while conduct may make the commitment sufficiently
specific

Implied Promise
- Definition: A promise inferred from conduct rather than stated
expressly
- Significance: In Harvey, the Dows’ approval of the site,
facilitation of permitting, and construction assistance could
imply a promise to convey that site
- Distinction: An implied promise is different from a mere
prediction or generalized hope because it must manifest a
commitment that justifies reliance

Reliance
- Definition: Action or forbearance induced by a promise
- Significance: Reliance connects the promise to the promisee’s
changed position and is required by Restatement (Second) § 90
- Distinction: The reliance must be more than a merely abstract
expectation and ordinarily must involve a definite and
substantial change of position

Detrimental Reliance
- Definition: Reliance that leaves the promisee worse off or
materially changes the promisee’s position because of the
promise
- Significance: Building Harvey’s approximately $200,000 house
was the central alleged detriment
- Distinction: The reading treats substantial detrimental
reliance as more important than minor inconvenience or an
uncompleted intention to act

Injustice
- Definition: The unfairness that results when a promise is not
enforced after foreseeable and substantial reliance

 ----------------------------------------------------------------
                           PAGE BREAK
----------------------------------------------------------------

- Significance: Under § 90, enforcement is justified only if
necessary to avoid injustice
- Distinction: Injustice is not established solely by the
existence of a promise or detriment; the circumstances must make
nonenforcement inequitable

Consideration
- Definition: The bargained-for exchange ordinarily required for
enforcement under conventional contract principles
- Significance: Harvey explains that promissory estoppel may
enforce a promise notwithstanding a lack of consideration
- Distinction: Promissory estoppel focuses on induced reliance
and injustice rather than on whether the promise was supported
by a bargain

Equitable Estoppel
- Definition: A traditional estoppel doctrine generally
associated with reliance on a misstatement of fact
- Significance: The reading contrasts equitable estoppel with
promissory estoppel and notes that equitable estoppel is
normally applied defensively
- Distinction: Promissory estoppel concerns an unfulfilled
promise, while equitable estoppel traditionally concerns an
inaccurate factual representation

Charitable Subscription
- Definition: A promise to make a charitable contribution
- Significance: The reading introduces charitable subscriptions
as an area where courts have sometimes enforced promises despite
weak consideration analysis
- Distinction: The assigned material identifies the issue but
does not provide the subsequent charitable-subscription case or
a complete governing test

Substantial Improvement

 ----------------------------------------------------------------
                           PAGE BREAK
----------------------------------------------------------------

- Definition: A valuable and permanent alteration or addition to
land made in reliance on a promise to convey it
- Significance: A house is treated in Harvey and Tozier as the
type of improvement that can make nonenforcement unjust
- Distinction: A substantial improvement is more than merely
occupying land or incurring a minor expense

General Promise
- Definition: A broad statement that an act will occur at some
unspecified time or concerning unspecified property
- Significance: The Dows’ general statements that Teresa would
eventually receive land were insufficient standing alone
- Distinction: A general promise may become enforceable when
coupled with conduct identifying a particular parcel and
inducing substantial reliance

Remedy Limited as Justice Requires
- Definition: The principle that a promissory-estoppel remedy
need not equal full expectation performance and may be tailored
to the justice of the case
- Significance: Restatement (Second) § 90 expressly provides
that the remedy may be limited, and the later history of Harvey
directs consideration of § 90 and Comment d
- Distinction: Promissory estoppel does not necessarily provide
the same remedy as a fully enforceable bargain

Reasonableness of Reliance
- Definition: Whether the promisee was justified in relying on
the promise and whether the manner and degree of reliance were
reasonable
- Significance: The family relationship and the parties’ conduct
are relevant to the inquiry
- Distinction: Reasonableness concerns both whether reliance was
justified at all and whether the extent and form of reliance
were justified
